FC.q: Who is responsible for most wills and estates law in Canada, and what is the result?
FC.a: The provinces and territories, because the Constitution gives them property and civil rights. The result is thirteen sets of rules, not one national law.

FC.q: Name three federal laws or programs that touch end-of-life planning.
FC.a: The Criminal Code (the framework for medical assistance in dying), the Income Tax Act (tax at death), and programs such as the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security.

FC.q: Who runs health care, hospitals, and vital statistics, and why does that matter for planning?
FC.a: The provinces and territories. It shapes palliative care, advance care planning, and who may make medical decisions for you.

FC.q: Which legal tradition does Quebec follow, and where are its estate rules mainly found?
FC.a: The civil law tradition, built on a written code. Its rules are found mainly in the Civil Code of Québec.

FC.q: What does Quebec call the person who settles an estate, and the document that names someone to act if you lose capacity?
FC.a: A liquidator, not an executor, and a mandate, not a power of attorney.

FC.q: What three forms of will does Quebec recognize?
FC.a: A notarial will (prepared by a notary), a holograph will (in your own handwriting), and a will made before two witnesses.

FC.q: Which Quebec wills must be verified before they take effect, and which need not be probated?
FC.a: Holograph and witnessed wills must go through verification. A notarial will does not need to be probated.

FC.q: What is the difference between a testator and an intestate person?
FC.a: A testator makes a will. A person who dies without a valid will dies intestate, and provincial or territorial law decides who inherits.

FC.q: What is the executor called in Ontario, in the British Columbia and Alberta legislation, and in Quebec?
FC.a: Estate trustee in Ontario, personal representative in British Columbia and Alberta, and liquidator in Quebec.

FC.q: Does “attorney” in a power of attorney mean lawyer? What is the property document called in each province?
FC.a: No. It is the person you choose to manage your finances. It is an enduring power of attorney in British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba, and a continuing power of attorney for property in Ontario.

FC.q: What are the personal care documents called in British Columbia, Alberta, and Ontario?
FC.a: A representation agreement in British Columbia, a personal directive in Alberta, and a power of attorney for personal care in Ontario.

FC.q: What is a deemed disposition?
FC.a: A tax rule that treats certain property as sold at death, even though no sale takes place. Chapter 12 covers it.

FC.q: How does the role of a notary differ in Quebec, British Columbia, and most other provinces?
FC.a: In Quebec, notaries are legal professionals and only they can prepare a notarial will. In British Columbia, notaries public may prepare certain documents within limits. Elsewhere a notary mainly witnesses and certifies, and a lawyer prepares the documents.

FC.q: Who belongs on your planning team?
FC.a: A lawyer, a financial advisor and accountant, your doctor or palliative care team, a funeral director, and the people who will act for you: your executor, attorney, and health care decision-maker.

FC.q: Why do a financial advisor and an accountant matter to a will?
FC.a: Wills interact with registered plans, insurance, and tax, and a professional with tax knowledge can help your executor avoid unpleasant surprises.

FC.q: What are the four pillars of a complete plan?
FC.a: Your property and wishes for it; planning for incapacity; how you wish to be cared for near the end of life; and what happens afterward.

FC.q: Which chapters cover each of the four pillars?
FC.a: Pillar 1: Chapters 2 to 4. Pillar 2: Chapters 5 and 6. Pillar 3: Chapters 7 and 8. Pillar 4: Chapters 9 to 12.

FC.q: What can a will do for you?
FC.a: It lets you decide who receives your property, choose the person who carries out your wishes, and name who you would like to care for young children.

FC.q: What are two limits of a will?
FC.a: It takes effect only at death, so it cannot help if you lose capacity while alive. It also does not control property passing outside it, such as joint property with survivorship and accounts with a named beneficiary.

FC.q: What are the three basic requirements of a formal will?
FC.a: Written, signed at the end by the will-maker, and witnessed by two adults who are present at the same time.

FC.q: What is a holograph will, and which provinces generally require witnesses instead?
FC.a: A will written entirely in your own handwriting and signed, usually without witnesses. British Columbia and Prince Edward Island generally require witnesses.

FC.q: Why should a holograph will be treated as an emergency measure?
FC.a: It is a common source of disputes: unclear wording, missing details, doubts about the handwriting, and some institutions are cautious about accepting it.

FC.q: What do British Columbia, Ontario, and Saskatchewan allow for electronic or remote wills?
FC.a: British Columbia permits electronic wills signed and witnessed electronically. Ontario allows video witnessing, but the will must still be a paper original signed in ink. Saskatchewan has passed legislation to allow electronic wills.

FC.q: Describe the signing and witnessing steps for a formal will.
FC.a: You sign at the end, or acknowledge your signature, in front of two witnesses present together. Each witness then signs in your presence. Witnesses are generally adults.

FC.q: What happens if a witness, or a witness’s spouse, is also a beneficiary?
FC.a: In many provinces the gift to that person can be cancelled, though the rest of the will stays valid. Choose two neutral adults.

FC.q: What safety net do some courts offer for a will that missed the formal rules, and why is it not a strategy?
FC.a: Ontario, British Columbia, and other provinces allow a judge to validate a document that clearly reflects the person’s wishes. It costs money, takes time, and invites disputes.

FC.q: What does testamentary capacity require, and which case do courts draw on?
FC.a: Understanding what making a will means and its effects, knowing roughly what you own, knowing who might expect to benefit, and reaching an orderly decision. Courts draw on Banks v Goodfellow.

FC.q: Is capacity a medical or a legal question, and when is it judged?
FC.a: A legal question, so an early diagnosis does not automatically remove it. It is judged when you give instructions and when you sign.

FC.q: What is undue influence, and how can you protect yourself?
FC.a: A will reflecting pressure from someone else, not your own wishes. Meet your lawyer alone, avoid having a beneficiary arrange or attend, and use an independent professional.

FC.q: What is the cleanest way to revoke a will?
FC.a: Make a new will that states it revokes all earlier wills. A will can also be revoked by a separate signed and witnessed document, or by deliberately destroying it with intent to cancel.

FC.q: What is a codicil, and when is replacing the will better?
FC.a: A formal amendment signed and witnessed like a will. For anything significant, replacing the will is clearer than a stack of amendments.

FC.q: How do marriage and divorce affect an existing will?
FC.a: Marriage cancelled a will in some provinces. Alberta and British Columbia do not, and Ontario stopped in 2022. Divorce in most provinces cancels gifts to, and the appointment of, a former spouse.

FC.q: Name four life events that should trigger a review of your will.
FC.a: Marriage or divorce, the birth or adoption of a child, the death of a beneficiary or executor, a move to a new province, the sale of a business, an inheritance, or a falling out.

FC.q: Where should the original will be kept?
FC.a: In a secure place your executor can reach, such as your lawyer’s vault or a home safe whose location is known. A safety-deposit box may be hard for others to open. Never staple or mark the original.

FC.q: What does an executor do?
FC.a: Finds and secures your property, pays your debts and taxes, and distributes what is left to the people named in your will.

FC.q: What qualities should you look for in an executor?
FC.a: Someone trustworthy, organized, and willing to do the work: honest, comfortable with paperwork, calm with banks and government offices, and likely to outlive you.

FC.q: When you name more than one executor, how must they usually act?
FC.a: Together, unless the will says otherwise. That adds a check on mistakes but can cause delay if they disagree.

FC.q: Why name an alternate executor, and what should you do before naming anyone?
FC.a: In case your first choice cannot or will not act. Speak to everyone you name before you write their name down.

FC.q: When might a trust company or lawyer be a sensible executor?
FC.a: For a large or complicated estate, or where family members may not get along, although they charge fees.

FC.q: What is the difference between a specific gift and the residue?
FC.a: A specific gift leaves a named item or sum to a named person. The residue is everything left after debts, taxes, specific gifts, and costs, usually divided into shares.

FC.q: What are two reasons a gift in a will can fail?
FC.a: A specific gift fails if you no longer own the item at death, and a gift may fail if the beneficiary dies before you. Name alternates for your beneficiaries.

FC.q: Can a pet inherit money? What works instead?
FC.a: No, because a pet is property. Leave the pet to a named person, often with money for its care, after asking that person first.

FC.q: What are three things to know about naming a guardian for minor children?
FC.a: The appointment is a request and the court decides by the child’s best interests; a surviving parent normally has priority; and some provinces limit its length. In Ontario it lasts only 90 days.

FC.q: Why can a guardian named in one parent’s will fail to work in a blended family?
FC.a: The child’s other living parent may be entitled to custody, so the appointment may not be effective for that child.

FC.q: What is a letter of wishes, and is it binding?
FC.a: A letter that tells guardians about schools, faith, routines, and values. It is not legally binding, but it can guide them.

FC.q: How do Quebec’s rules for naming a tutor work?
FC.a: A parent can name more than one tutor for a child’s property, but only one individual or couple for the child’s person. If none is named, a court appoints one.

FC.q: Why would a minor’s inheritance need a testamentary trust?
FC.a: A minor cannot hold a large inheritance. Without a trust the money often goes to a public trustee and is paid out in one lump sum at the age of majority.

FC.q: What is the tax cost of most testamentary trusts?
FC.a: Since 2016 they are taxed at the top rate on income they keep. Exceptions are a graduated rate estate in its first 36 months and a qualified disability trust.

FC.q: How can a will protect both a surviving spouse and children from an earlier relationship?
FC.a: Give the spouse a right to live in the home, or to receive income, for life, with the capital going to the children afterward.

FC.q: What goes wrong when a parent adds an adult child to a bank account or house title?
FC.a: Courts presume no gift to that child alone, so the asset may be treated as belonging to the estate, causing disputes, unexpected tax, and probate fees. Put any intended gift in writing with legal advice.

FC.q: Who decides who gets money from a registered plan or life insurance policy: your will or the plan’s form?
FC.a: The plan’s form, because the money passes directly to the named beneficiary outside your estate. For a TFSA, naming a spouse as successor holder rather than beneficiary can affect its tax-free status.

FC.q: What is an intestacy, and can a judge adjust the formula?
FC.a: Dying without a valid will. Legislation sets a fixed list of relatives and a fixed formula, and a judge has no power to adjust it to what the person would have wanted.

FC.q: Who runs an estate when there is no will?
FC.a: A relative must apply to the court to be appointed administrator, usually a spouse or adult child, who may have to post a bond. In Ontario this is an estate trustee without a will.

FC.q: What is the broad intestacy pattern across common-law Canada?
FC.a: The spouse is first. With children, the estate is shared, often with a preferential share first. With no spouse, children inherit equally. Then parents, siblings, more distant relatives, and finally the Crown.

FC.q: In Ontario, what does a married spouse receive on an intestacy for deaths on or after March 1, 2021?
FC.a: The first $350,000 of the estate. If the estate is smaller and there are children, the spouse takes everything, and with no children the spouse takes the whole estate.

FC.q: In Ontario, how is an estate above the $350,000 preferential share divided?
FC.a: With one child, the spouse and the child each take half the remainder. With more than one child, the spouse takes one-third and the children share two-thirds.

FC.q: How does British Columbia’s preferential share work?
FC.a: The spouse receives $300,000 if all the children are also the spouse’s, or $150,000 if some are not. The remainder is split half to the spouse and half among the children.

FC.q: How does Alberta divide an intestate estate with a spouse and children?
FC.a: If all children are shared with the spouse or adult interdependent partner, that person gets the entire estate. Otherwise the survivor receives the greater of $150,000 or half of the net value.

FC.q: How does Quebec divide an intestate estate with a spouse?
FC.a: Fixed fractions. With children, the spouse receives one-third and the children two-thirds. With no children, the spouse receives two-thirds and parents or siblings share one-third.

FC.q: Does an Ontario common-law partner inherit on an intestacy? What other routes exist?
FC.a: No, the rules apply only to legally married spouses. A financially dependent partner may bring a dependant’s support claim, and may receive property passing outside the estate.

FC.q: How do British Columbia and Alberta treat unmarried partners on an intestacy?
FC.a: In British Columbia, two years in a marriage-like relationship generally gives the same rights as a married spouse. In Alberta, an adult interdependent partner has the same rights as a spouse.

FC.q: How are de facto spouses treated in Quebec, and what did the 2024 reform change?
FC.a: They have long not been heirs. Bill 56 reportedly creates a limited exception for a partner who is a parent of the deceased’s child and has lived with them over a year. A notary should confirm whether it applies.

FC.q: Who is a dependant in Ontario, and how long do you have to bring a claim?
FC.a: A spouse, parent, child, or sibling to whom the deceased was providing or obliged to provide support just before death. A claim generally must start within six months of the grant of probate.

FC.q: Who can ask a British Columbia court to vary a will, and what is the deadline?
FC.a: A spouse or a child, including an adult child, if the will does not make adequate, just, and equitable provision. A claim generally must start within 180 days of the grant of probate.

FC.q: How does Quebec protect support claims while preserving testamentary freedom?
FC.a: A spouse, child, or parent owed support can claim a contribution within six months of the death, capped at half what they would have received on an intestacy, less what they received.

FC.q: Do stepchildren inherit on an intestacy?
FC.a: No, stepchildren are not recognized as heirs. Whether they could bring a support claim depends on the province and the facts.

FC.q: What is the difference between a support claim and a will contest?
FC.a: A support claim accepts the will but asks the court to change what it provides. A contest argues the will should not count at all.

FC.q: What are the main grounds for contesting a will, and what are the costs?
FC.a: Failure to follow formal rules, lack of testamentary capacity, undue influence, forgery or fraud. Litigation is slow and expensive, the loser may pay part of the winner’s costs, and it can strain families.

FC.q: Why is a plan for incapacity as important as a will, and why is being family not enough?
FC.a: You may become unable to manage your affairs while alive, and a will works only at death. Banks, pension plans, and government offices want written proof of authority, and a joint account does not cover property in one person’s name.

FC.q: What happens if you become incapable and have no power of attorney?
FC.a: Your family has no authority to sell your house or move your investments. They must ask a court to appoint a guardian, which is what a power of attorney is designed to avoid.

FC.q: What is a power of attorney, and does “attorney” mean a lawyer?
FC.a: A document in which you, the grantor, name another person, the attorney, to act for you in financial matters. The attorney is not necessarily a lawyer, and what they do binds you legally.

FC.q: How does a general power of attorney differ from an enduring or continuing one?
FC.a: A general power ends when you lose capacity, which is when it would be most useful. An enduring or continuing power is written to keep working after you lose capacity.

FC.q: What is the difference between an immediate and a springing power of attorney?
FC.a: An immediate power can be used as soon as it is signed. A springing power takes effect only when a trigger occurs, usually the loss of capacity.

FC.q: In Alberta, when can an enduring power start, and who declares incapacity if the document names no one?
FC.a: On signing, on a set date, or on a specified event. If it depends on incapacity and names no one, two medical practitioners must make written declarations.

FC.q: What are the trade-offs of immediate and springing powers, and what is a common middle path?
FC.a: Immediate powers are easy for banks to accept but risk misuse. Springing powers reassure but can cause delay. A middle path is to sign an immediate power and leave it with your lawyer, with written instructions about when to release it.

FC.q: What can an attorney do unless you limit the power?
FC.a: Generally anything you could do with your property if you were capable, except make a will.

FC.q: What should you look for in an attorney, and what is the risk of naming joint attorneys?
FC.a: Someone honest, organized, comfortable with money, able to act at a distance if need be, and willing. Joint attorneys check each other but can deadlock.

FC.q: Why must you name a backup attorney?
FC.a: If the first attorney dies, is unwell, or declines and there is no alternate, the document may stop working when you need it.

FC.q: What duties does an attorney owe you, and what should the document say about gifts and payment?
FC.a: To act in your interest, keep your property separate from their own, and keep records. Rules on gifts, loans, and pay differ by province, so say clearly what you allow.

FC.q: How can you monitor an attorney, and what are the warning signs of trouble?
FC.a: Have statements sent to a second person, require accounting to a named family member, or name a monitor. Warning signs are unexplained account changes, reluctance to share information, and sudden unusual spending.

FC.q: What are British Columbia’s signing rules for a power of attorney, and what is the Nidus registry?
FC.a: You must be 19 or older and capable, and sign before two witnesses, or one if a lawyer or notary. The attorney and certain relatives and employees cannot witness. Nidus is a registry where documents can be recorded.

FC.q: What is a Quebec protection mandate, and what is homologation?
FC.a: A document naming mandataries to look after your person and property if you become incapable. It has no effect until the Superior Court declares you incapable and homologates, or officially approves, the mandate.

FC.q: What does a Quebec homologation application need, and what happens afterward?
FC.a: The mandate or a certified copy, a medical assessment, a psychosocial assessment, and register search certificates. The Curateur public then records it in the register, and the court may set up a tutorship if it cannot homologate.

FC.q: Can an ordinary power of attorney replace a protection mandate in Quebec?
FC.a: No. An ordinary power of attorney stops being valid when the person becomes incapacitated.

FC.q: What is guardianship of property, and what are its disadvantages compared with a power of attorney?
FC.a: A court appoints someone to manage the property of a person who cannot. In Ontario anyone can apply with a management plan. It is slower, costs more, makes finances public, and the person appointed may not be your choice.

FC.q: What is your legal right regarding medical treatment, and what is a substitute decision-maker?
FC.a: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment, and professionals need informed consent. A substitute decision-maker exercises that right when capacity is lost. Without planning, the law picks the person from a fixed list.

FC.q: How is capacity defined in health care, and how is it judged?
FC.a: The ability to understand the information relevant to a decision and appreciate what is likely to follow. Capacity is presumed, judged for each decision, and can change over time.

FC.q: What are the two kinds of personal care document?
FC.a: One names a person to decide for you. The other records your instructions about treatment and care. Some provinces use one document for both, and others use two.

FC.q: What are the personal care documents called in Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, and Quebec?
FC.a: Ontario: power of attorney for personal care. British Columbia: representation agreement, plus a separate advance directive. Alberta: personal directive. Quebec: advance medical directives and the protection mandate.

FC.q: What are the age rules for personal care documents in British Columbia and Alberta?
FC.a: In British Columbia you must be 19 or older and capable, and your representative must be 19 or older. Alberta allows a capable person aged 18 or older. British Columbia also has a limited section 7 agreement.

FC.q: What are the witnessing rules for an Alberta personal directive and a British Columbia section 9 agreement?
FC.a: Alberta: dated and signed in front of a witness, who cannot be the agent, the agent’s partner, or the maker’s partner. British Columbia: two witnesses, or one if a lawyer or notary.

FC.q: Does a power of attorney for property cover health decisions?
FC.a: In most provinces, no. Property and personal care are separate legal authorities, and a bank-focused document will not let anyone consent to treatment.

FC.q: Who decides for you in Ontario if you have named no one?
FC.a: A ranked list under the Health Care Consent Act: a guardian of the person, an attorney for personal care, a Board-appointed representative, a spouse or partner, a child or parent, a parent with access only, a sibling, then any other relative. The Public Guardian and Trustee decides if equals disagree.

FC.q: Who decides in British Columbia if you have no representative or directive?
FC.a: A provider picks the first who qualifies: spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent, grandchild, other relative, close friend, related by marriage, then a person appointed by the Public Guardian and Trustee. They must be 19 or older, willing, capable, available, and in contact with you in the past year.

FC.q: Who consents for you in Quebec if you cannot?
FC.a: The mandatary if there is a homologated mandate, the tutor under tutorship, or otherwise your spouse, then a close relative, then a person with a special interest. The Curateur public acts only as a last resort.

FC.q: What happens in Alberta if you have no personal directive?
FC.a: The service provider must usually inform the nearest relative or a person listed in the regulations, and a court can appoint a guardian. Confirm the relative list with a lawyer.

FC.q: What makes a good personal care decision-maker, and why ask before naming one?
FC.a: Someone who stays calm, understands your values, speaks up to doctors, and acts on your wishes. A person who agreed in advance knows the role and could say no while you can still choose someone else.

FC.q: In what order is a decision-maker guided?
FC.a: By your instructions first, then what you said while capable, then your known values and beliefs, and finally your best interests.

FC.q: What can a British Columbia representative not do unless the agreement clearly allows it?
FC.a: Request medical assistance in dying, and consent to treatments that are not medically necessary, such as research, sterilization, or organ or tissue donation.

FC.q: How should you share a personal care document, and when does an Alberta personal directive take effect?
FC.a: Give copies to your decision-maker, backup, doctor, and a relative, because registries usually record only that a document exists. An Alberta directive takes effect after you are declared incapable, and your authority returns if you recover.

FC.q: How are disagreements about care resolved?
FC.a: Keep records, ask for a meeting with the care team, and seek ethics or patient-relations support first. Ontario’s Consent and Capacity Board can review them, and in Quebec a court order is needed to authorize care an incapable person refuses categorically.

FC.q: When should you review a personal care document, and how do you revoke it?
FC.a: Every few years and after big events such as a divorce, a death of the decision-maker, a new diagnosis, or a move. Revoke by signing a new document and giving the new version to everyone with a copy.

FC.q: What is advance care planning?
FC.a: A process of reflection and communication, not a single form: thinking about what matters, learning, choosing someone to speak for you, talking, and, if you wish, writing it down.

FC.q: What are the five Speak Up steps?
FC.a: Think, learn, decide, talk, and record. Recording is optional, and the written plan may be called an advance directive or medical directive.

FC.q: When does a written plan matter, and is it only for the old or ill?
FC.a: It matters only if you cannot make your own health care decisions, and until then your own consent counts. It is for everyone, since accidents and strokes happen to anyone, and it can be changed as often as you like.

FC.q: How should you start the conversation about your wishes?
FC.a: With values, not medical terms: what a good day looks like, what you fear, whether you want more time with limits or less time with comfort, and what must be present for life to feel worthwhile.

FC.q: What medical questions should you think about?
FC.a: Whether you would want CPR, a breathing machine, artificial feeding, dialysis, or a move to a care home, and whether the answers change if you are seriously ill. Your doctor or nurse practitioner can explain each.

FC.q: How does a wish differ from a medical order? Give examples.
FC.a: A written plan records what you want. A medical order is written by a doctor or nurse practitioner and followed by teams and first responders, such as Alberta’s Goals of Care Designation, British Columbia’s No CPR Form, or a MOST.

FC.q: Can medical orders be cancelled, and does a No CPR order mean no care?
FC.a: Yes, at any time. In British Columbia, speak with your physician, destroy the signed form, and tell everyone with a copy. No CPR does not mean no care: pain management, antibiotics, dialysis, and nutrition can continue.

FC.q: What are Quebec’s advance medical directives?
FC.a: A form stating your wishes about specific treatments if you become unable to consent. When written while capable, the substitute must follow it when the physician considers the care necessary, even if the substitute disagrees.

FC.q: What is palliative care, and is it only for the last days of life?
FC.a: No. It focuses on quality of life for people with a progressive, life-limiting illness, including symptom management and emotional, social, and spiritual support, and can be given alongside treatment that aims to slow or cure the illness.

FC.q: Where can palliative care be provided, and when should you ask for it?
FC.a: At home, in hospital, in long-term care, or in a hospice residence, depending on province and community. Ask your doctor early rather than waiting to be offered it.

FC.q: What is a hospice, and how does it differ from a nursing home?
FC.a: A place or program providing comfort-focused care at the end of life, often homelike with round-the-clock care. It is not a nursing home, and treatment does not simply stop.

FC.q: How are hospice costs covered?
FC.a: Provincial plans usually cover inpatient hospice care in hospital, including medicines and supplies. Home care may be covered by home care programs, but medicines and equipment may not be. Long-term care residents generally pay part of their care.

FC.q: How limited is hospice access in Canada?
FC.a: Best practice is about seven beds per 100,000 people, and Canada averages about 3.97. Ask early, visit if you can, and put your preference in writing.

FC.q: What does dying at home usually require?
FC.a: A capable caregiver, home care nursing, equipment such as a hospital bed, an emergency plan, and an agreed backup such as a hospice bed.

FC.q: What are the three Employment Insurance caregiving benefits?
FC.a: Compassionate care: up to 26 weeks for end-of-life care. Family caregiver for adults: up to 15 weeks. Family caregiver for children: up to 35 weeks for a critically ill child under 18.

FC.q: What are the EI caregiving eligibility points, and what other support exists?
FC.a: The caregiver need not live with the person or be related, and the condition must be certified by a doctor or nurse practitioner, with end-of-life care stating a significant risk of death within 26 weeks. Respite, counselling, and bereavement services are also available.

FC.q: What is medical assistance in dying, and which law governs it?
FC.a: A lawful medical service in which a physician or nurse practitioner, at a capable adult’s voluntary request, provides or prescribes medication that causes death. The federal Criminal Code sets the rules, and provinces organize delivery.

FC.q: How does MAID differ from refusing treatment, palliative care, or a No CPR order, and must any practitioner provide it?
FC.a: None of those is MAID. In MAID the medication causes death. No individual practitioner must provide it, though health systems must have ways to connect patients with willing providers.

FC.q: What are the federal eligibility conditions for MAID?
FC.a: Live in Canada and be eligible for government-funded health services, be at least 18 and capable, have a grievous and irremediable condition, and make a voluntary request with informed consent.

FC.q: What is a grievous and irremediable condition?
FC.a: A serious illness, disease, or disability in an advanced state of decline that cannot be reversed, causing unbearable suffering that cannot be relieved in ways the person finds acceptable.

FC.q: What are the two pathways, and what share of 2024 provisions did each represent?
FC.a: Track one: natural death reasonably foreseeable, about 95.6 percent. Track two: not reasonably foreseeable, with extra safeguards, about 4.4 percent.

FC.q: Is mental illness alone a qualifying condition?
FC.a: Not currently. On October 7, 2026, the federal justice minister announced an indefinite exclusion, with legislation not yet tabled then, so confirm the current law. People with mental illness plus another qualifying condition are assessed on that condition.

FC.q: Can you withdraw a MAID request?
FC.a: Yes, at any time, up to the final moment. A request is not a commitment.

FC.q: What are the written request requirements?
FC.a: Signed and dated before one independent witness who is at least 18, cannot benefit from the death, cannot be an unpaid caregiver, and cannot own or operate the facility where the person lives or is cared for.

FC.q: Who assesses a MAID request?
FC.a: Two independent practitioners, physicians or, where a province permits, nurse practitioners. The second must give a written opinion confirming eligibility.

FC.q: What extra safeguards apply on the second pathway?
FC.a: An assessor with expertise in the condition or a consultation, discussion and consideration of ways to relieve suffering, and an assessment period of at least 90 days unless the person is at immediate risk of losing capacity.

FC.q: What is a waiver of final consent, and when is it available?
FC.a: A limited exception, available only if natural death is reasonably foreseeable and specific conditions, including a written arrangement with the practitioner, were met while the person had capacity.

FC.q: How does Quebec’s medical aid in dying differ?
FC.a: It follows the Act respecting end-of-life care, with a government form and a second practitioner’s written confirmation. Neurocognitive disorders such as Alzheimer’s qualify as serious and incurable illnesses, while severe and chronic depression does not.

FC.q: Can a power of attorney or personal directive authorize MAID, and what is the position on advance requests?
FC.a: Generally no, because MAID requires your own capable, voluntary request and consent. Federal advance requests are not yet law, and in October 2026 the government announced coming legislation. Confirm the current position with a lawyer.

FC.q: What did Quebec allow from October 30, 2024?
FC.a: People diagnosed with a serious and incurable illness that will lead to incapacity, such as early-stage Alzheimer’s disease, can make an advance request for medical aid in dying.

FC.q: How should you prepare to talk with family and the care team about MAID?
FC.a: Hold an honest conversation early and repeat it. Many provinces have coordination services, and a practitioner who objects must help connect you with someone who will consider the request.

FC.q: Where can you turn if you are struggling with thoughts of ending your life outside this process?
FC.a: Call or text 9-8-8, the national Suicide Crisis Helpline, at any time in Canada.

FC.q: Who has authority over funeral arrangements in Ontario, and what must that person show?
FC.a: The order begins with the estate trustee (the executor), then the spouse, adult children, and parents. The person arranging must show photo identification and proof of authority.

FC.q: Who decides in British Columbia, and what if equals disagree?
FC.a: Usually the executor, then the spouse, adult children, adult grandchildren, and further relatives. The eldest decides among equals, and one who wants sole control can apply to the Supreme Court.

FC.q: Why is naming an executor also a decision about your funeral, and what weight do written wishes carry?
FC.a: The executor holds the first right to decide. In British Columbia written instructions must be followed unless unreasonable, impractical, or a hardship, and elsewhere courts and providers give great weight to clear wishes.

FC.q: Why should funeral wishes not be only in your will?
FC.a: Wills are often read after the funeral, and a safe-deposit box may be sealed. Put them in a separate note your executor and family can see right away.

FC.q: How does Quebec treat written funeral wishes?
FC.a: They are given weight, and a notary can help record them in your will or separately. The rules on who decides without instructions differ from the common-law provinces.

FC.q: What are the main burial and cremation choices?
FC.a: Burial in a plot, mausoleum, or natural or green burial ground. After cremation, ashes may be buried, placed in a columbarium niche, kept, scattered, or a combination. Ontario also recognizes alkaline hydrolysis, and does not require embalming.

FC.q: Where may ashes be scattered in Ontario?
FC.a: On private property with the owner’s consent, or on unoccupied Crown land, including water, if no signs prohibit it. Municipal land requires checking local by-laws, which may ban scattering in parks.

FC.q: How can Ontario families manage funeral costs?
FC.a: Buy caskets and monuments from unlicensed businesses if the provider will accept them, expect licensed providers to offer a range of prices, and apply to the municipality for help before signing a contract.

FC.q: How do pre-planning and pre-paying differ?
FC.a: Pre-planning means deciding and recording what you want. Pre-paying means paying in advance. You can plan without prepaying, and most providers keep plans on record at no cost.

FC.q: What must an Ontario prepaid contract contain, and how is the money protected?
FC.a: The purchaser, recipient, provider, services and supplies, terms, cancellation rights, commissions, and taxes. Money goes through a trust or insurance, and licensed providers are covered by the Prepaid Funeral Services Compensation Fund. The amount is guaranteed for contracts from July 1, 2012.

FC.q: What are the cancellation rules in Ontario and British Columbia?
FC.a: Ontario: all money back within 30 days, then a fee of 10 percent of the trust amount up to $350. British Columbia: 15 days to cancel for any reason with a full refund.

FC.q: What does Quebec’s Consumer Protection Act restrict for prearranged funerals?
FC.a: Vendors may not solicit unless asked, may not solicit by phone or in hospitals or care centres, and may not approach someone recently bereaved or ill. A home visit must be requested 24 hours ahead, between 9:30 a.m. and 10 p.m., for no more than two hours.

FC.q: How do you register as an organ and tissue donor in Ontario, and is a donor card enough?
FC.a: You must be at least 16, using your health card online, in person, or by mail. A signed card is not enough, because only the registry record confirms consent. The Trillium Gift of Life Network checks it, and families almost always honour it.

FC.q: How does whole body donation differ from organ and tissue donation?
FC.a: Whole body donation supports medical teaching and research through a school of anatomy. Organ and tissue donation helps living recipients. They are different programs, and one decision does not cover the other.

FC.q: Why tell family and doctors about a donation decision, and what must be coordinated with MAID?
FC.a: Donation usually needs prompt action at or near death. Combining MAID with donation requires careful coordination, so talk to your team early.

FC.q: What should a short funeral plan cover?
FC.a: Burial or cremation, type of service, where to be buried or ashes placed, preferred provider, any prepaid contract, and religious or cultural practices. A page or two is plenty.

FC.q: Who normally pays for the funeral, and how can you spare your family?
FC.a: The estate pays, but a family member often pays first and is repaid. A prepaid contract or small dedicated account spares the family, and a copy of any contract should go to your executor.

FC.q: What happens first after an expected and an unexpected death in Ontario?
FC.a: For an expected death, the family contacts the doctor who was caring for the person. For an unexpected death they call emergency services, or the coroner if unclear. A doctor or coroner completes the Medical Certificate of Death.

FC.q: Whom should you tell first, and what should you avoid in the first days?
FC.a: The funeral provider, close family, the executor, and the employer or care facility. Avoid large decisions such as selling a house or cancelling accounts, secure the home, and be cautious about publicizing the funeral date.

FC.q: How is a death registered in Ontario, and in what order do the documents follow?
FC.a: A funeral director and an informant complete the Statement of Death for the municipal clerk. Registration comes first, then the burial permit and the death certificate.

FC.q: Who can order a certified death certificate in Ontario, and why order several?
FC.a: Only the next of kin or the executor, with no limit on copies. Banks, insurers, pension plans, and land registries may each need an original or certified copy. Check names, dates, and marital status as soon as it arrives.

FC.q: How are deaths recorded in Quebec, and whom should QPP recipients contact?
FC.a: In the civil status register, with information from the funeral director or a family member. Those who received Quebec Pension Plan benefits should also contact Retraite Québec.

FC.q: Which three federal offices are time-sensitive, and why?
FC.a: The Canada Revenue Agency, the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security, and the Canada Disability Benefit if received. Delays can cause overpayments the estate must repay.

FC.q: What happens to CPP and OAS payments after a death?
FC.a: Report the death to Service Canada with the SIN ready. The estate is entitled to the payment for the month of death, and payments issued after that must be returned, even if already cashed.

FC.q: What other federal steps does the chapter list?
FC.a: Vital statistics notifies the SIN program in provinces. Tell EI and the Canadian Dental Care Plan, mail the passport to the Passport Program, withdraw immigration applications, notify Equifax and TransUnion, and forward mail.

FC.q: What are two Ontario provincial steps after a death?
FC.a: Return an accessible parking permit to ServiceOntario within 30 days, and cancel the driver’s licence at a ServiceOntario centre, where a refund may apply if six or more months remain and there are no outstanding fines.

FC.q: What is the CPP death benefit for deaths on or after January 1, 2025, and when should the executor apply?
FC.a: A one-time $2,500 plus a possible $2,500 top-up, for a maximum of $5,000. Federal guidance advises applying within 60 days, and processing normally takes six to twelve weeks.

FC.q: Who qualifies for the CPP death benefit and its top-up?
FC.a: The deceased must have contributed for at least one-third of the years in their contributory period, with a minimum of three, or for ten years. The top-up requires no prior CPP or QPP disability or retirement benefit and no eligible survivor’s pension recipient.

FC.q: What is the CPP survivor’s pension for someone aged 65 or older, and who counts as a common-law partner?
FC.a: 60 percent of the contributor’s retirement pension, if the survivor receives no other CPP benefit. A common-law partner lived with the contributor in a conjugal relationship for at least one year.

FC.q: What are the back payment, remarriage, and children’s benefit rules for the survivor’s pension?
FC.a: Back payments cover only up to twelve months, so apply early. Remarriage does not end the pension, and children under 25 may qualify for children’s benefits.

FC.q: What does Retraite Québec provide, and what does a surviving spouse generally receive from a workplace pension?
FC.a: The Quebec Pension Plan death, survivor’s, and orphan’s benefits. For a death in retirement, a surviving spouse generally receives a joint and survivor pension of at least 60 percent, unless the spouse agreed to less.

FC.q: How should you organize the first weeks, and do early tasks need probate?
FC.a: Use a notebook with a page per organization, keep reference numbers, scan every letter, and designate one master record keeper. Most tasks need only a death certificate and identification, but keep a list of those waiting for a grant.

FC.q: How do you protect the estate from fraud after a death?
FC.a: Scammers read obituaries and pose as creditors. Agencies do not demand gift card or wire payment, a legitimate creditor writes a claim, and unusual contacts go to the executor or lawyer.

FC.q: What other sources of death benefits should you check?
FC.a: Workplace pensions and group benefits, life insurance (needs a claim form and death certificate), Veterans Affairs Canada for Armed Forces families, and the Memorial Grant for First Responders. The OmbudService for Life and Health Insurance can help search for a lost policy.

FC.q: What does probate do, and what is the document called in Ontario and British Columbia?
FC.a: The court process confirms the will is valid and the executor has authority. Ontario: Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee. British Columbia: grant of probate.

FC.q: Which assets often need probate, and which usually do not?
FC.a: Sole-name real estate and accounts above an institution’s threshold often need it. Jointly owned property with survivorship, and accounts or policies with a named beneficiary, generally pass outside the estate. Ask each institution.

FC.q: What is Ontario’s Estate Administration Tax?
FC.a: Nothing on estates of $50,000 or less, then $15 per $1,000 above that, with the value rounded up to the nearest $1,000. An estate of $240,000 pays $2,850.

FC.q: What counts toward the value for Ontario’s tax?
FC.a: Ontario real estate less mortgages and liens, bank and investment accounts, vehicles, and other property. It excludes real estate outside Ontario, assets with named beneficiaries, and jointly owned assets that pass automatically. Funeral costs and debts cannot be deducted.

FC.q: How do other provinces’ probate fees compare?
FC.a: British Columbia: $6 per $1,000 to $50,000, $14 above, plus a $200 filing fee. Alberta: tiered flat fees to a $525 maximum. Saskatchewan: $7 per $1,000. Manitoba abolished its fee in 2020. Confirm current rates, since they change.

FC.q: What must be filed in Ontario within 180 days, and what penalties apply for false information?
FC.a: An Estate Information Return, even if the value is zero. Penalties include a fine of at least $1,000 and up to twice the tax, up to two years in prison, or both, and records must be kept four years.

FC.q: What does it mean that an executor is a fiduciary?
FC.a: The executor must act with loyalty and care for beneficiaries and creditors. The role is not honorary, and an executor can be personally liable for mistakes, even decisions made in good faith without proper care.

FC.q: What are the executor’s basic duties?
FC.a: Secure the property, locate and list assets and debts, open a separate estate account kept apart from personal money, keep detailed records, notify beneficiaries, deal with creditors, have tax returns filed, and distribute according to the will.

FC.q: Which executor actions commonly draw claims?
FC.a: Favouring one beneficiary, using estate property personally, mixing estate and personal money, and reimbursing undocumented expenses. Regular neutral updates reduce suspicion.

FC.q: What are the steps of a Quebec liquidator, and what is the risk of early distribution?
FC.a: Obtain proof of death, have non-notarial wills verified, publish notices, prepare a signed inventory, file returns, obtain federal and Quebec certificates, pay debts, and give a final account. Distributing before the certificates may mean personal liability for unpaid taxes.

FC.q: In what order does an estate pay debts?
FC.a: The funeral and administration costs are priority expenses, then the deceased’s debts, including taxes, loans, and credit cards, before gifts. Rules differ by province, so a doubtful estate calls for a lawyer first.

FC.q: What is the most dangerous distribution mistake, and what protects the executor?
FC.a: Distributing too early. If a debt or tax bill appears, the executor may pay personally. The federal clearance certificate is the main protection against income tax, and a reserve should be held until debts and taxes are clear.

FC.q: How are gifts distributed, and what can a dissatisfied beneficiary do?
FC.a: Specific items go to the named people, cash gifts are paid, and the residue is divided. The executor prepares an account and seeks approval and a signed release. A beneficiary may ask the court to review the accounts, called passing the accounts in some provinces.

FC.q: On what does executor compensation depend, and what should the executor keep?
FC.a: The will, the quality of the work, and the accounts that support it. Courts consider the estate’s size and complexity, time and skill, and care shown. Keep a time and task log from the start.

FC.q: May a named executor refuse, and who can end an appointment?
FC.a: A named person may refuse if they have not begun acting. An executor who cannot continue can ask the court to be replaced, and beneficiaries can ask the court to remove one who is not doing the job.

FC.q: Why do estates often take about a year or more?
FC.a: Delays come from waiting for tax clearance, selling property, locating assets, or resolving disputes. Plan for patience, keep beneficiaries informed, and avoid pressure to distribute early.

FC.q: Does Canada have an inheritance or estate tax?
FC.a: No. Beneficiaries do not normally pay tax on what they receive. The tax arises on the deceased’s final return, and the executor pays it from the estate before distribution.

FC.q: What period does the final return cover, and what becomes of later income?
FC.a: January 1 to the date of death. The estate then becomes a separate taxpayer for income arising after death and may need its own return.

FC.q: What first steps does the CRA ask of an executor?
FC.a: Report the death as soon as possible, then register as the legal representative. Processing generally takes about 28 business days, and the CRA does not send confirmation.

FC.q: What are the final return deadlines, including for business owners?
FC.a: Death January 1 to October 31: April 30 of the next year. Death November 1 to December 31: six months after death. Business owners: June 15 for deaths up to December 15, but the payment deadline does not move.

FC.q: What is a return for rights or things?
FC.a: An optional return covering amounts the person had earned but not yet received at death, which may reduce tax. Its deadline is the later of one year after death or 90 days after the final return’s notice of assessment.

FC.q: What penalties apply to a late return with a balance owing?
FC.a: 5 percent of the balance plus 1 percent for each full month late, up to 12 months. Unpaid balances accrue compound daily interest from the day after the due date.

FC.q: What is the deemed disposition, and how much of a capital gain is taxed?
FC.a: On death a person is treated as having sold all capital property at fair market value, so gains are taxed on the final return. One-half of a gain is included in income, because a proposal to raise that was cancelled in 2025.

FC.q: How are registered plans taxed at death, and when can tax be deferred?
FC.a: The full value of an RRSP or RRIF is normally added to income in the year of death. A rollover to a surviving spouse or partner’s plan can defer tax, and similar rules may apply to a dependent child or grandchild.

FC.q: How does the principal residence exemption work?
FC.a: A gain on a home that qualified as a principal residence is generally exempt, claimed on the final return. Only one home can be designated for a given year, which matters with a house and a cottage.

FC.q: Why obtain date-of-death valuations, and how do joint ownership and designations affect tax?
FC.a: Fair market value that day sets the gain on the final return and the beneficiary’s cost. Assets passing by joint ownership or designation can still generate tax on the final return, and the executor may recover it from recipients.

FC.q: When must an estate file a T3?
FC.a: If it earns income, such as interest or dividends, or distributes property. If a CPP or QPP death benefit is its only income, the beneficiary can report it on their own return.

FC.q: What is a graduated rate estate, and how is it designated?
FC.a: For up to 36 months an estate is taxed at normal graduated rates. Tick the box on the first T3, and the executor can choose a year-end within 12 months of death. Only one such estate is allowed per person.

FC.q: When is the T3 due, and what is the late penalty?
FC.a: 90 days after the estate’s year-end, or after final distribution if the trust ends. A late T3 draws $25 per day, minimum $100, maximum $2,500, even if no tax is owing.

FC.q: What does a clearance certificate do?
FC.a: If an executor distributes while the CRA is owed money, the executor is personally liable up to the value distributed. The certificate confirms the tax is paid or secured and shifts remaining liability to the estate and recipients.

FC.q: When should the executor request the certificate, and how long does it take?
FC.a: Only after all returns are filed and assessed and taxes paid or secured. Use the TX19, not sent with the returns. The CRA acknowledges within 45 days, and the assessment can take up to 120 days or longer.

FC.q: What must a Quebec liquidator obtain before distributing, and what may be paid first?
FC.a: A certificate authorizing distribution from Revenu Québec, whatever the value. Before it is issued, urgent expenses of up to $12,000 for the death or the property may be paid, and a partial certificate may be issued.

Q.ti: Provincial jurisdiction and the family example
Q.q: Margaret lives in Hamilton, Ontario, her son lives in Calgary, and her daughter lives in Montreal. Which statement correctly describes the law that governs each person’s will?
o: Ontario rules for Margaret, Alberta rules for her son, Quebec civil law for her daughter
One national wills law applied the same way to all three family members
Federal law for Margaret, with provincial law only for her two children
Ontario law for all three, because Margaret’s own will was signed first and others copy it
Q.e: Provinces govern property and civil rights, so each person follows the rules of their own province. Quebec uses civil law. Territories make their own laws under delegated powers, producing thirteen sets of rules.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly matches a subject with the level of government that mainly governs it?
o: Wills rules are federal, while the Income Tax Act is provincial or territorial
Criminal Code framework for medical assistance in dying is federal; hospitals are provincial
Medical assistance in dying is provincial, and public hospitals are federal
Taxes at death are provincial only, and Canada Pension Plan rules are territorial
Q.e: Parliament makes the Criminal Code and the Income Tax Act and runs programs such as the Canada Pension Plan. Provinces and territories run health care, hospitals, and vital statistics, which shapes palliative care and medical decision-making.

Q.ti: Territorial authority and the count of jurisdictions
Q.q: Yukon, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut make their own laws on wills and estates. What is the source of that power, and how many sets of rules result across Canada?
o: Powers delegated by Parliament; thirteen sets of rules
Their own constitutions; ten sets of rules
The provincial legislatures; twelve sets of rules
A federal wills statute; one national set of rules
Q.e: The territories legislate under powers that Parliament has delegated to them. With ten provinces and three territories, Canada has thirteen sets of rules on wills and estates rather than one.

Q.ti: Provincial differences and the common mistake
Q.q: A reader in Alberta follows advice written for Ontario about witnesses and document names. Which idea from Chapter 1 does this illustrate, and what is the remedy?
o: The federal override of provincial law; no further checking is required
The Quebec readers rule; read only the Quebec paragraphs in the book
The common mistake of using another province’s advice; check your own place’s rules
Territorial delegation of powers; ask Parliament which rules apply to you
Q.e: Rules on witnesses, forms, and even document names differ across the country. The chapter warns against reading advice written for another province as if it applied to yours and recommends checking your own place’s rules.

Q.q: Quebec runs its own pension plan, while other provinces use the Canada Pension Plan. What does this show about how rules fit together in Canada?
o: Quebec has no link to federal programs or to federal tax law
A federal program may have a Quebec counterpart; your location decides which applies
Every province now runs its own separate pension plan and tax regime
The Quebec Pension Plan replaces the Income Tax Act inside Quebec
Q.e: The guide describes a federal rule on top, a provincial or territorial rule underneath, and your own location deciding which version applies. Quebec’s pension plan is one example, while the federal Income Tax Act still applies.

Q.ti: The Civil Code and Quebec vocabulary
Q.q: Where are Quebec’s rules on wills, inheritance, and mandates for incapacity mainly found, and which two terms does Quebec use for the people involved?
o: In a provincial Wills Act; executor and mandate
In the federal Criminal Code; liquidator and power of attorney
In the Civil Code of Québec; liquidator and mandate
In court decisions alone; executor and power of attorney
Q.e: Quebec follows the civil law tradition, built on a written code. The person who settles an estate is a liquidator, and the document naming someone to act if you lose capacity is a mandate, not a power of attorney.

Q.q: Outside Quebec, how did the law on wills develop, and what now sits on top of it?
o: Court decisions over centuries; statutes such as a Wills Act now sit on top
A written code adopted all at once; court decisions now sit on top of it
Notarial practice over centuries; federal regulations now sit on top of that practice
Provincial charters first; the Civil Code now sits on top of them
Q.e: The common law tradition grew out of court decisions over centuries. Statutes such as a Wills Act or an Estates Act now sit on top of it, whereas Quebec’s civil law is built on a written code.

Q.q: Which Quebec will form does not need to be probated, and what must the other two forms go through?
o: The holograph will; a notary’s seal on each copy
The witnessed will; registration with the Chambre des notaires
The notarial will; a verification process
The notarial will; nothing, since all three forms take effect at once
Q.e: A notarial will is prepared by a notary, who keeps the original, and it needs no probate. Holograph and witnessed wills must go through a verification process before they take effect.

Q.ti: Holograph and witnessed wills in Quebec
Q.q: One Quebec resident writes her entire will by hand and signs it. Another signs hers before two witnesses. How are these wills classified, and what applies to both?
o: Both notarial; neither needs any verification before taking effect
Holograph and witnessed; both need verification before taking effect
Holograph and witnessed; only the holograph needs verification first
Witnessed and notarial; a notary keeps both of the originals
Q.e: A holograph will is written entirely in the testator’s hand and signed. A witnessed will is signed before two witnesses. Both must go through a verification process before they take effect, unlike a notarial will.

Q.q: Elena lives in Ontario, owns a cottage in Quebec, and has a sister in Montreal. What does the chapter suggest she do about the Quebec paragraphs?
o: Skip them, because only Quebec residents are ever affected by them
Ignore them, because Ontario law governs property wherever it sits
Read them last, after every other chapter and Appendix A
Read them too, since her plan may touch both legal systems
Q.e: Quebec readers paragraphs are meant first for people who live in Quebec, but the chapter says that anyone who owns property in Quebec or has family there should read them too, since the plan may touch both systems.

Q.q: Margaret dies owning a house, savings, and some debts. What is her estate, and what is the person who makes a will called?
o: Only the house and savings she owned; the beneficiary
Everything she owned, ignoring all her debts; the executor
Everything owned at death, less what is owed; the testator
Only the property named in her will; the intestate person
Q.e: Your estate is everything you own at death, less what you owe. The person who makes a will and sets out who receives property and who carries out the wishes is called the testator.

Q.q: A man dies without a valid will. Who decides who inherits, and what is he called?
o: The executor he chose; he died intestate
The court registrar; he died a testator
Federal law across Canada; he died a beneficiary
Provincial or territorial law; he died intestate
Q.e: If you die without a valid will you die intestate, and provincial or territorial law decides who inherits. The executor’s role is to carry out a will, so it cannot decide in the absence of one.

Q.ti: Terms for the person who carries out a will
Q.q: Which pairing matches the person who carries out a will with the title used in the legislation of that place?
o: Liquidator in Ontario; personal representative in Quebec only
Estate trustee in Ontario; personal representative in British Columbia and Alberta
Personal representative in Quebec; liquidator in Alberta and Ontario
Estate trustee in Alberta; attorney in British Columbia and liquidator in Ontario
Q.e: The everyday word is executor, but the formal title varies: estate trustee in Ontario, personal representative in British Columbia and Alberta legislation, and liquidator in Quebec. Attorney refers to a power of attorney, not a will.

Q.ti: Power of attorney terms and capacity
Q.q: Walter names his niece in a document so she can manage his finances if he loses capacity. In Ontario, what is it called, and does “attorney” mean she must be a lawyer?
o: A continuing power of attorney for property; no, attorney means the person appointed
An enduring power of attorney for property; yes, only lawyers are appointed
A representation agreement; no, attorney means the person appointed
A personal directive; yes, only licensed lawyers can ever be appointed to serve
Q.e: Capacity is the ability to understand and appreciate decisions. In Ontario the finance document is a continuing power of attorney for property, while British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba say enduring. Attorney here does not mean lawyer.

Q.q: Which statement correctly defines probate and deemed disposition?
o: Probate treats property as sold at death; deemed disposition confirms a will
Probate confirms a will; deemed disposition treats property as sold at death
Probate means burial or cremation; deemed disposition means a sale to heirs
Probate is a medical option; deemed disposition is a funeral choice
Q.e: Probate is the court process that confirms a will and gives the executor authority, though not every estate needs it. Deemed disposition is a tax rule, covered in Chapter 12, that treats certain property as sold at death.

Q.q: Who can prepare a notarial will in Quebec, and who else may prepare estate documents there?
o: Only a lawyer; notaries merely witness and certify documents
Either a notary or a lawyer, as they are interchangeable here
Only a notary; Quebec lawyers may not prepare any estate documents
Only a notary; Quebec lawyers may also prepare other estate documents
Q.e: In Quebec, notaries are legal professionals who prepare wills and mandates, and only a notary can prepare a notarial will. Quebec lawyers can also prepare estate documents, so a person may choose either.

Q.ti: Notaries in British Columbia and elsewhere
Q.q: How does a British Columbia notary public differ from a notary public in most other provinces, and what do BC notaries generally leave to lawyers?
o: BC notaries may prepare some estate documents; complex or disputed matters go to lawyers
BC notaries only witness documents; every will must go to a lawyer for drafting
BC notaries act as Quebec notaries do; notarial wills go to lawyers
BC notaries replace lawyers fully; no estate matters go to lawyers
Q.e: BC notaries public are regulated professionals who may prepare documents such as wills and powers of attorney within limits. In most other provinces a notary mainly witnesses and certifies, and a lawyer prepares estate documents.

Q.ti: Financial and tax advisors on the team
Q.q: Why does the chapter include an accountant or financial advisor on the planning team, and what can they help the executor avoid?
o: They must co-sign the will; they help avoid needing any witnesses at all
Wills interact with registered plans, insurance, and tax; they help avoid surprises
They store the original will; they help avoid probate altogether
They replace the lawyer; they help avoid paying legal fees entirely
Q.e: Wills interact with registered plans, insurance, and tax. A professional with tax knowledge can help a future executor avoid unpleasant surprises, a point that Chapter 12 explains further.

Q.ti: Team members who act for you
Q.q: The chapter says a plan that none of the key people know about cannot be carried out. Who are those people, and what does that imply?
o: Executor, attorney, and health care decision-maker; tell them about your plan
Lawyer, notary, and accountant; keep the plan private from all family members
Funeral director, doctor, and advisor; give them the original documents
Beneficiaries only; they need not know their roles until later
Q.e: The people who will actually act for you are your executor, your attorney, and your health care decision-maker. If none of them knows the plan exists, it cannot be carried out.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly matches a team member with what they contribute?
o: A funeral director drafts your will; a family doctor files your final tax return
A palliative care team keeps the original will; a notary explains disposition options
A family doctor names your executor; a funeral director witnesses your will
A funeral director explains disposition options; a palliative care team explains medical choices
Q.e: Your family doctor, nurse practitioner, or palliative care team can help you understand medical choices, and a funeral director can explain your options for disposition. Lawyers draft documents and accountants advise on tax.

Q.q: Which pillar covers beneficiary designations on registered plans and insurance, and which chapters cover it?
o: Pillar 2, Incapacity; Chapters 5 and 6
Pillar 3, Care and Final Wishes; Chapters 7 and 8
Pillar 1, Your Property; Chapters 2, 3, and 4
Pillar 4, After a Death; Chapters 9 through 12
Q.e: The first pillar covers your property and your wishes for it: the will, the way assets are owned, and beneficiary designations on accounts such as registered plans and insurance. Chapters 2, 3, and 4 cover it.

Q.q: Powers of attorney, mandates, directives, and representation agreements belong to which pillar, and what situation do they address?
o: Pillar 1, Your Property; how assets pass after your death occurs
Pillar 3, Care and Final Wishes; how you want care near the end
Pillar 4, After a Death; how the estate is settled afterward
Pillar 2, Incapacity; a time when you are alive but cannot decide
Q.e: The second pillar is planning for a time when you are alive but unable to decide for yourself, for both money and personal care. Chapters 5 and 6 cover these documents.

Q.q: Medical assistance in dying belongs to which pillar, and what else does that pillar include?
o: Pillar 3, Care and Final Wishes; advance care planning and palliative care
Pillar 4, After a Death; funeral arrangements and estate administration work
Pillar 2, Incapacity; court guardianship and powers of attorney for property and care
Pillar 1, Your Property; trusts, joint ownership, and beneficiary designations
Q.e: The third pillar is how you wish to be cared for near the end of life: advance care planning, palliative and hospice care, and, for those who are eligible, medical assistance in dying. Chapters 7 and 8 cover it.

Q.q: Margaret has a will signed fifteen years ago, no one named to manage her finances or health decisions, and no one who knows her funeral wishes. What does the chapter conclude?
o: All four pillars are complete, because she has a signed will
Two pillars are solid, and only her funeral wishes are missing
She has one pillar, partly built
None of the pillars stand, because her will is now out of date
Q.e: Her old will covers part of the first pillar but is out of date. With no attorney, no health decision-maker, and no funeral wishes known, the other pillars are missing. She has one pillar, partly built.

Q.q: Why does the chapter sort the planning tasks into pillars, and what does a gap in one pillar do?
o: It ranks tasks by cost; a gap in one affects only that pillar
It assigns each pillar to one lawyer; a gap in one cancels the others
It separates provinces from territories; a gap in one has no effect
It keeps the documents from feeling overwhelming; a gap in one weakens the others
Q.e: The pillars help keep the many documents and decisions from feeling overwhelming. Together they hold up a complete plan, and a gap in any one of them leaves the others weaker.

Q.q: Margaret’s will leaves everything to her husband, who has died, and says nothing about a replacement executor. What does this show about wills?
o: Wills expire automatically ten years after they are signed in all provinces
It reflects the family when written, so an old will needs review
A will stays valid only while the named spouse is still alive
A will cannot name an executor or a replacement for that executor
Q.e: A will speaks for you after death, but it reflects the family situation when it was written. Margaret’s will names her late husband as executor and does not say who should step in, so she needs to update it.

Q.q: A will takes effect only at death. What does that mean for someone who later loses the ability to manage their affairs while alive?
o: It takes effect early once capacity is lost, so it helps right away
The executor automatically takes over managing the finances while the person lives
It cannot help; powers of attorney and personal care documents are needed
A court applies the will to the person’s affairs at once
Q.e: A will takes effect only at death, so it cannot help if you lose the ability to manage your affairs while alive. That is the subject of Chapters 5 and 6, which cover powers of attorney and personal care.

Q.q: Which of Walter’s assets would usually pass outside his will?
o: A car left to his niece and furniture left to his son by the will
A jointly held home with survivorship and a policy with a named beneficiary
Any asset he owns alone, because only joint assets pass by will
A savings account with no beneficiary named and a bequest in the will
Q.e: A will does not control everything you own. Property held jointly with a right of survivorship, and accounts or policies with a named beneficiary, usually pass outside the will. Chapter 3 shows how to coordinate them.

Q.q: Without a will, what decides who receives a person’s property, and why is that a drawback?
o: The executor’s own discretion, which may favour the closest friend or any relative
A fixed formula in provincial or territorial law that ignores the family’s circumstances
A court’s case-by-case review, which always follows what the person wanted
A federal formula that applies the same way in every province
Q.e: Without a will, provincial or territorial law makes the choices using a fixed formula that cannot take your family’s circumstances into account. Chapter 4 explains how that formula works.

Q.q: Which set lists choices a will lets you make?
o: Who manages your money while alive, who makes health decisions, and who treats you
Who receives your property, who pays your taxes, and which court hears your case
Who witnesses your will, who keeps your pension, and who sets your probate fee
Who receives your property, who carries out your wishes, and who may care for children
Q.e: A will lets you decide who receives your property, choose the person who will carry out your wishes, and, if you have young children, say who you would like to care for them.

Q.q: What are the basic requirements of a formal will?
o: Written, signed at the end, and witnessed by two people present together
Typed, notarized by a lawyer, and filed with the court registry office
Handwritten, signed at the end, and seen by one witness afterward
Written, signed anywhere, and registered with the province before death
Q.e: The formal will is written, usually typed, signed by the will-maker at the end, and signed in front of two witnesses who are present at the same time. Written, signed, and witnessed is a simple way to remember it.

Q.q: A resident of Alberta and a resident of Prince Edward Island each handwrite a will and sign it without witnesses. What does the chapter say about each?
o: Prince Edward Island recognizes holograph wills; Alberta generally requires witnesses
Both provinces recognize holograph wills made without any witnesses
Alberta recognizes holograph wills; Prince Edward Island generally requires witnesses
Neither province recognizes any handwritten will under any circumstances
Q.e: Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Quebec recognize holograph wills. British Columbia and Prince Edward Island generally require witnesses.

Q.q: Holograph wills are free and fast. Why does the chapter call them an emergency measure rather than a plan?
o: They are illegal in most provinces and cannot be used at all
They must always be probated twice before they take any effect
They cost much more than formal wills to prepare with a lawyer
Unclear wording, missing details, and doubtful handwriting can cause costly court disputes
Q.e: Holograph wills are tempting because they are free and fast, but unclear wording, missing details, and doubts about the handwriting can lead to costly court proceedings, and some financial institutions are cautious about accepting them.

Q.q: Which statement about Quebec notarial wills and will registers is correct?
o: Two witnesses prepare and keep it; courts alone record all wills in Canada
The will-maker prepares it alone; registers exist only for holograph wills
A notary prepares and keeps it; registers can record wills and mandates
A lawyer prepares and files it; registers record only witnessed wills
Q.e: A notarial will is an authentic act prepared by a notary with a witness present, and the notary keeps the original. The Chambre des notaires and the Barreau keep registers where wills and protection mandates can be recorded.

Q.q: Which pairing about electronic wills is correct, according to the chapter?
o: British Columbia permits electronic wills; Ontario needs a paper original in ink
Ontario permits electronic wills; British Columbia allows video witnessing only
Both provinces accept any online template signed without any witnesses
Neither province lets technology play any part in making or witnessing a will
Q.e: British Columbia permits electronic wills signed and witnessed electronically. Ontario permits witnesses to watch the signing by video, but the will must still be a paper original signed in ink. Technology is changing unevenly.

Q.q: Which description of the signing and witnessing sequence for a formal will is correct?
o: The witnesses sign first, and then the will-maker signs later in private
The will-maker signs before one witness; a second signs the next day
The will-maker signs alone; two witnesses sign it the following day
Will-maker signs before two witnesses together; each witness then signs in their presence
Q.e: The will is in writing, and you sign it at the end, or acknowledge your signature, in front of two witnesses present together. Each witness then signs in your presence. Witnesses generally must be adults.

Q.q: Elena’s neighbour witnesses her will and also receives a gift under it. What may happen in many provinces, and what do some provinces allow?
o: The whole will becomes invalid and no court can preserve the gift
The gift can be cancelled and the will stands; some courts may preserve it
The gift doubles in value while the will stays valid without a court
Nothing changes, because neighbours may always witness a will and also inherit
Q.e: In many provinces the gift to a witness, or a witness’s spouse, can be cancelled even though the rest of the will remains valid. Some provinces let a court preserve it, but that takes an application and cannot be counted on.

Q.q: Which choice of witnesses does the chapter recommend?
o: Two adult children who are both named as beneficiaries in the same will
Two neutral adults, such as colleagues or neighbours, not named in the will
One beneficiary and one neighbour who is not named in the will
Any two relatives, since family witnesses are always acceptable in practice
Q.e: Witnesses generally must be adults, and in most provinces they should not be beneficiaries or married to one. The chapter recommends two neutral adults, such as colleagues or neighbours, and avoiding family members named in the will.

Q.q: A will does not meet the formal rules but clearly reflects the person’s wishes. What may courts in Ontario and British Columbia do, and why is it not a strategy?
o: A judge may validate it; the application costs money, takes time, invites disputes
The registrar validates it automatically; the process is quick but expensive
The executor may declare it valid; no court is ever involved at all
Only Quebec courts may validate it; other provinces never allow validation
Q.e: Ontario, British Columbia, and other provinces now allow a judge to validate a document that does not meet the formal rules if it clearly reflects the person’s wishes. It is a safety net, because the application is costly, slow, and can provoke disputes.

Q.q: Priya moves to a new province. A will valid where it was made is generally respected elsewhere. What does the chapter still recommend?
o: Do nothing, because the will becomes void as soon as she moves provinces
Re-sign it before a notary in Ottawa, which cures every problem
Convert it to a holograph will, which every province accepts
Have it checked, especially if she owns real property in the new province
Q.e: A will that is valid where it is made is generally respected elsewhere, yet the chapter says that moving to a new province is a good reason to have the will checked, especially if you own real property there.

Q.q: Which elements does the test from Banks v Goodfellow ask about?
o: Understanding of the will, knowledge of property, awareness of claimants, and orderly decision-making
Whether the will-maker was over seventy, owned a home, and had a lawyer present
Whether the will-maker could write, drive, and manage a bank account alone
Whether the will-maker had no diagnosis, had family nearby, and used a template
Q.e: Courts draw on this nineteenth-century English case, which asks about understanding of the will’s meaning and effects, knowledge of property, awareness of those who might expect to benefit, and an orderly decision unaffected by delusions or illness.

Q.q: Walter has early memory loss. Is capacity a legal or a medical question, and what effect does a diagnosis have?
o: Medical; any diagnosis of memory loss removes capacity automatically
Legal; a diagnosis alone does not automatically remove capacity
Legal; any diagnosis of memory loss removes capacity automatically
Medical; a doctor’s letter settles the question once it is written
Q.e: Capacity is a legal question, not a medical one, so a diagnosis such as early memory loss does not automatically remove it. A doctor’s letter can help but does not settle the question.

Q.q: When is capacity judged, and what did Walter’s lawyer do to protect his will?
o: Only at death; his lawyer met him with a relative present at midday
Only on the day he hires a lawyer; the lawyer relied on his diagnosis
At any point in the past year; the lawyer asked a beneficiary to attend
At instructions and signing; his lawyer met him alone and recorded his answers
