Q.e: Capacity is judged when you give your instructions and when you sign. Walter is clear in the mornings, so his lawyer met him alone early, asked him to describe his family and property, and recorded the answers as possible evidence.

Q.q: What is undue influence, and who tends to be affected by it?
o: A mistake in the wording of a will, mostly in holograph wills
Pressure from someone else, often where an older person depends on a carer
A tax paid on a gift to a witness, mostly on large estates
A rule requiring a doctor’s approval, mostly for people in hospital
Q.e: Undue influence means the will reflects pressure from someone else rather than the will-maker’s own wishes. It tends to arise where an older person depends on someone for care or help.

Q.q: Which steps does the chapter suggest to guard against undue influence, and what is the role of a doctor’s letter?
o: Have a beneficiary arrange the meeting; a doctor’s letter settles the question
Use a template prepared by a beneficiary; a doctor’s letter is never useful
See the lawyer alone, with an independent professional; a doctor’s letter only helps
Bring a relative to the meeting; a doctor’s letter is always required
Q.e: Meet your lawyer alone, avoid having a beneficiary arrange or attend the meeting, and have the will prepared by an independent professional. If capacity is in doubt, a physician’s assessment can help, though it does not settle the question.

Q.q: What is the cleanest way to revoke a will, and why is crossing things out risky?
o: Cross out the old clauses and initial them; such changes are always valid and safe
Tell the executor orally; handwritten changes then strengthen the original will itself
Make a new will stating it revokes earlier wills; crossed-out changes may be invalid
Staple a note to the will; the note automatically revokes the document
Q.e: The cleanest way is a new will stating that it revokes all earlier wills. Crossing things out or adding handwritten notes to a signed will is risky, because the changes may be invalid and can cast doubt on the original.

Q.q: What is a codicil, and when does the chapter suggest replacing a will instead?
o: A formal amendment signed and witnessed like a will; replace for anything significant
A handwritten note needing no witnesses; replace it only after a death occurs
A document revoking all earlier wills; replace it for small changes only
A court order changing the will; replace it for any amendment at all
Q.e: A codicil is a formal amendment signed and witnessed in the same way as a will. For anything significant, replacing the will is usually clearer, because a stack of amendments invites confusion about which document says what.

Q.ti: Marriage and divorce effects on wills
Q.q: Which statement about marriage, divorce, and an existing will matches the chapter?
o: Marriage cancels a will in every province; divorce never affects a will at all
Ontario still cancels a will on marriage; divorce cancels the whole will
Alberta cancels a will on marriage; divorce cancels only the executor’s fee
Alberta does not cancel on marriage; divorce usually cancels gifts to a former spouse
Q.e: Marriage has historically cancelled a will in some provinces, but Alberta and British Columbia do not, and Ontario stopped in 2022. Divorce more consistently cancels gifts to a former spouse and that person’s appointment as executor.

Q.q: Which pairing gives a good trigger for reviewing a will and sound advice about storing it?
o: A new phone number; keep the original in a box only a bank can open
A birthday ending in zero; staple new changes to the signed original
A business sale; store the original in a lawyer’s vault and tell the executor
A move within the same street; give the original to a beneficiary quietly
Q.e: Life events should trigger a review, including a business sale, a child’s birth, or a move. The original should be kept where the executor can reach it, such as a lawyer’s vault, and the executor should be told where it is.

Q.q: Margaret’s fifteen-year-old will names her late husband as her only beneficiary and executor. Which course fits the chapter best?
o: Replace it with a new will revoking earlier wills and tell her executor
Leave it as it is, because it still exists and was properly signed
Cross out her husband’s name and initial the change in the margin
Add a handwritten note to the original naming her son instead
Q.e: Margaret’s will no longer fits her family, and a significant change is better made by a new will that revokes earlier wills. She should also tell her executor where the signed original is stored.

Q.q: Margaret is choosing an executor. What does the executor do, and what should guide her choice?
o: Inherits the whole estate automatically; whoever loves her most deeply
Supervises the funeral only; whoever lives nearest to her home address
Files the will and then steps aside; the oldest relative available
Finds property, pays debts, distributes the rest; trustworthiness and willingness
Q.e: The executor steps into your shoes, finding and securing property, paying debts and taxes, and distributing what remains. The chapter advises choosing for trustworthiness, organization, and willingness rather than for who loves you most.

Q.q: A will names two executors. How must they usually act, and what is the practical effect?
o: Separately unless a court says otherwise; faster, but a weaker check
Together only if both live in one province; no effect on speed
Together unless the will says otherwise; an added check, but possible delay
One after the other by age; no effect on mistakes or delay
Q.e: More than one executor usually must act together unless the will says otherwise. That adds a check on mistakes but can cause delay if they disagree. The chapter also advises naming at least one alternate.

Q.q: Which statement about who may serve as an executor is correct?
o: Only a lawyer or a trust company may ever serve in this role
A non-beneficiary only, since beneficiaries face a conflict of interest
A relative who lives in the same province as the testator
An adult, who may also be a beneficiary; a trust company may serve
Q.e: An executor must be an adult, and the age of majority is 18 in some provinces and 19 in others. An executor can also be a beneficiary, and many people name a spouse or adult child, a friend, a lawyer, or a trust company.

Q.ti: Distance and alternates in Margaret’s choice
Q.q: Margaret asks her daughter in Montreal to act as executor and names her son in Calgary as alternate, though neither lives near Hamilton. How does the chapter treat distance?
o: As a legal barrier that disqualifies both of her children
As a practical factor to weigh, not a legal barrier
As irrelevant, since executors never deal with local offices
As a reason to name only a trust company instead
Q.e: Margaret picks her daughter because she is better with paperwork and names her son as alternate. The chapter calls distance a practical factor to weigh, not a legal barrier, and recommends speaking to anyone before naming them.

Q.q: In Quebec, what is the person who settles an estate called, and what happens if the will names no one?
o: A liquidator; the heirs choose one
An executor; a court appoints one at once
A tutor; the notary decides who acts
A liquidator; the Crown appoints a public official
Q.e: In Quebec the person who settles your estate is called a liquidator. You can name one or more in your will, and if you name no one, the heirs choose.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly defines a specific gift and the residue of an estate?
o: Any gift left to charity; everything the will gives to the executor
A named item or sum for a person; what remains after debts and gifts
Only gifts of money; only the property sold during probate work
A gift to a child; a gift to a spouse under intestacy rules
Q.e: A specific gift leaves a named item or sum, such as jewellery or $10,000, to a named person. The residue is everything left after debts, taxes, specific gifts, and costs, usually divided into shares.

Q.q: In which situations might a specific gift in a will fail?
o: The gift is over $10,000, or the beneficiary lives outside the province
The item is jewellery, or the beneficiary is a close relative of the giver
The will names alternates, or the item is fully insured at death
The item is no longer owned at death, or the beneficiary dies first
Q.e: A specific gift fails if you no longer own the item when you die, and a gift may fail if the beneficiary dies before you. Some provinces save certain gifts to children or grandchildren, but you should not count on them.

Q.q: Why does the chapter say the residue often matters more than any single gift, and how is it usually divided?
o: It catches whatever was not mentioned; it is usually split into shares
It is taxed first; it is always paid to the executor as a fee
It is the only part a court reviews; it passes to the Crown
It covers only debts; it is divided by the court among creditors
Q.e: Because the residue catches everything you did not mention, it often matters more than any single gift. It is usually divided into shares, such as equally among your children.

Q.q: Priya wants to provide for the family dog in her will. What approach does the chapter say works?
o: Name the dog as a beneficiary so it receives a share of the residue
Leave the pet to a person you have asked, with money for its care
Leave money directly to the dog and name a neighbour as trustee
Rely on informal wishes, which courts always enforce against the family
Q.e: In law a pet is property, so it cannot inherit money or be a beneficiary. What works is leaving the pet to a named person, often with a gift for its care. Ask the person first, because no one can be forced to take a pet.

Q.q: Which details should a will give for a charitable gift, and what other benefit can giving bring?
o: The charity’s full legal name and registration number; it can reduce estate tax
Only the charity’s popular name; it removes any need for an executor
The charity’s street address; it ends any claim by family members
The charity’s website; it avoids probate fees on the whole estate
Q.e: Use the charity’s full legal name and registration number so your executor can identify it, and check that it still exists. Gifts to charity can reflect your values and reduce the tax your estate pays.

Q.q: Which statement about naming a guardian for minor children in a will is correct?
o: A command, so a court must approve it exactly as written by the parents
Valid only if both parents die together on the same day or night
Binding on a surviving parent, who loses any priority afterward
A request, not a command; a court decides using the child’s best interests
Q.e: Parents of minor children can name a guardian in their wills, but the appointment is a request. A court has the last word and decides based on the child’s best interests.

Q.ti: Priority and time limits on guardianship
Q.q: If one parent dies and the other survives, who has priority, and what limit applies to a guardian’s appointment in Ontario?
o: The named guardian takes over at once; Ontario’s appointment lasts for life
The surviving parent loses priority; Ontario’s appointment lasts one year
The surviving parent normally has priority; Ontario’s appointment lasts only 90 days
The guardian has priority; Ontario’s appointment needs no court application
Q.e: A surviving parent normally has priority, so the appointment matters most when both parents have died. In Ontario the appointment lasts only 90 days after death, so the guardian must promptly apply to court.

Q.q: Arjun and Chloe each have another living parent. What does that mean for a guardian named in Priya’s will?
o: It may not work for Arjun if his father is alive and entitled to custody
It always overrides the other living parent’s rights over each child in the family
It applies only to Maya, the one child that Priya and Daniel share together
It is void in Alberta unless Daniel signs it as a witness to Priya’s will
Q.e: A guardian named in Priya’s will may not be effective for Arjun if his father is alive and entitled to custody, and the same holds for Chloe. A lawyer can help match each plan to each child’s situation.

Q.ti: Choosing guardians and a letter of wishes
Q.q: What does the chapter advise about choosing guardians, and what is a letter of wishes?
o: Choose the oldest relative; the letter is legally binding on the guardians chosen
Choose only blood relatives; the letter replaces the guardian clause in the will
Choose the nearest neighbour; the letter is filed with the court registry office
Choose for values, stability, and willingness; the letter guides but is not binding
Q.e: Choose guardians for their values, stability, and willingness, not only family ties, ask them first, and name an alternate. A letter of wishes covers schools, faith, and routines. It is not legally binding, but it can guide them.

Q.q: In Quebec, what is a guardian of a child called, and whom may a parent name?
o: A liquidator; more than one for the child’s person, but one for property
A tutor; more than one for property, but one person or couple for the child
A tutor; one person only for property and any number for the child’s person
A mandatary; one person for both the property and the child’s person
Q.e: In Quebec the word for a guardian is tutor. A parent can name more than one tutor for a child’s property but only one individual or couple for the child’s person. If none is named, a court appoints one.

Q.q: A minor child inherits a large sum and the will names no trustee. What often happens?
o: The executor invests it until the child turns 25 and then pays it out slowly
The court splits it into yearly payments, which continue automatically for life
A public trustee holds it until the age of majority, then pays out a lump sum
The money passes to the other beneficiaries named in the will instead
Q.e: A minor cannot hold a large inheritance directly. Without direction in the will, the money often goes to a public trustee and is paid over in one lump sum at the age of majority. Public trustees charge fees and have limited discretion.

Q.q: What is a testamentary trust, and what can its terms do for a child?
o: A trust created during life; it ends once the will is signed
A trust created by the will, naming a trustee and setting when money is used
A court account for minors; it pays everything out at 18 or 19
A tax form filed by executors; it gives the child a lump sum
Q.e: A testamentary trust is created by your will. It names a trustee, who may be your executor or someone else, and sets out how and when money is used, for example for education and health costs now and in portions later.

Q.q: Since 2016, how are most testamentary trusts taxed, and what exceptions does the chapter mention?
o: Graduated rates on all income; exceptions for any trust whose trustee is a lawyer
Exempt from tax entirely; exceptions apply to any trust above $100,000 in assets
Top rate on income kept; no exceptions exist for any kind of trust at all
Top rate on income kept; exceptions for a graduated rate estate and a qualified disability trust
Q.e: Most testamentary trusts are taxed at the top rate on income they keep, rather than at graduated rates. Exceptions exist for a graduated rate estate during its first 36 months and for a qualified disability trust.

Q.q: Daniel wants to provide for Priya yet protect an inheritance for Chloe. Which common solution does the chapter describe?
o: Leave everything to Priya outright and trust her to pass something on later
Let the spouse live in the home or take income for life; children get capital
Leave everything to Chloe, even if Priya then has nowhere to live
Name Priya executor and give the home to a trust company at once
Q.e: The will can give a surviving spouse the right to live in the home, or to receive income, for life, with the capital going to the children afterward. It depends on trustworthy trustees and must work alongside family property and support laws.

Q.q: The chapter’s Common Mistake warns against leaving a large gift “to my children” with no plan for a minor child’s share. What can result?
o: It may go to a public trustee and be paid out all at once
The gift is automatically void, so the residue passes to the Crown instead
The money is held in a court account until the child turns 30
The executor must keep the whole share as payment for managing it
Q.e: Without a trustee named in the will, a minor’s share may go to a public trustee and then be paid out all at once at the age of majority, which is 18 or 19 depending on the province.

Q.q: A parent adds an adult child to a bank account to avoid probate. What do courts presume, and what can follow?
o: A gift to that child was intended; no tax or dispute can follow from it
The account is void; the bank must freeze it for the next two years
No gift to that child alone was intended; disputes, tax, and probate fees may follow
The child holds it for charity; the parent keeps all the tax benefits
Q.e: Courts presume that the parent did not intend a gift to that child alone, so the asset may belong to the estate unless a gift is clearly shown. The result can be a dispute, a tax bill, and probate fees.

Q.ti: Property that passes outside the will
Q.q: Which items would usually pass outside a person’s will?
o: A watch left to a niece in the will and the remaining residue
A savings account with no beneficiary named and a gift in the will
A home held jointly with survivorship and an RRSP with a named beneficiary
A car owned alone and a sum left to charity in the will
Q.e: Property held jointly with a right of survivorship passes automatically to the surviving owner, and RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, pensions, and life insurance with a named beneficiary pass directly to that person.

Q.q: Who decides who receives money in a registered plan or insurance policy, and what risk does the chapter describe?
o: The plan’s form, not the will; an old form may pay a former partner
The will, in every case; an old designation is cancelled automatically by law
The executor, using discretion; an old designation is ignored if it seems unfair
A court, after probate; an old designation is replaced by the intestacy rules
Q.e: For RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, pensions, and life insurance, the plan’s form, not your will, decides who gets the money. A designation made decades ago and never updated can send a large sum to a former partner.

Q.q: For a TFSA, what can naming a spouse as successor holder rather than beneficiary affect?
o: Whether the executor receives a fee from the account
Whether probate is avoided for the whole estate
Whether the account keeps its tax-free status
Whether the spouse must have been married for two years
Q.e: Naming your spouse as successor holder, rather than as beneficiary, can decide whether the account keeps its tax-free status. Quebec has its own rules for some designations, so Quebec residents should ask their notary.

Q.ti: Coordinating the will with other property
Q.q: After listing every account, policy, and property with its owner and beneficiary, what does the chapter recommend?
o: Replace the will with the list, since designations always override wills entirely
Compare the will with the list so they fit together, and review after changes
File the list with the court, which will reconcile it with the will
Give the list to every beneficiary so each can change their own designation
Q.e: The list and the will should fit together, and each should be reviewed after any major change in your family. Some property passes outside the will, so the two must work as one plan.

Q.q: When a person dies without a valid will, what decides the division of the estate, and can a judge adjust it?
o: The family agrees how to divide the property; a judge can adjust any share
The oldest relative decides; a judge can change shares to match likely wishes
Legislation sets a fixed list of relatives and formula; a judge cannot adjust it
The executor chosen by the court decides; a judge reviews each gift made
Q.e: An intestacy follows a fixed list of relatives and a fixed formula set by legislation. The formula is the same whether the family is close or estranged, and a judge has no power to adjust it to match what the person would likely have wanted.

Q.q: Who runs an estate when there is no will, and what may the court require?
o: The eldest child takes over automatically; the court requires a public trustee
The bank manager takes over at once; the court requires a lawyer’s letter
A relative applies to be appointed administrator; the court may require a bond
A neighbour is appointed; the court requires two witnesses to every payment
Q.e: Nobody has been chosen to run the estate, so a relative must apply to the court to be appointed administrator. The court usually appoints a spouse or an adult child and may require a bond, which insures the estate against mistakes or misuse.

Q.q: A will fails to dispose of some property because a beneficiary died first and the will had no backup. What happens to that portion?
o: The whole will becomes void and the estate is reset
It is divided as though there were no will at all
It passes to the executor as payment for acting as executor
It is shared equally among all of the remaining beneficiaries named
Q.e: An intestacy can be partial. If a will fails to dispose of some property, that portion is divided as though there were no will at all. For this reason a will that looks complete can still leave gaps.

Q.q: If Margaret’s old will were set aside, who would inherit, and why does the chapter call this an accident?
o: Her son alone, because he is older; it would follow her stated wishes
Her former colleague and children equally; it would follow her old habits
Her two adult children in equal shares; it would follow a formula, not her decision
Her daughter alone, because she is better with paperwork; it would follow a court’s choice
Q.e: Her two adult children would share equally because she is widowed with no other close family. That may sound fair, but it would be an accident rather than a decision, since only a will can express choices such as unequal shares.

Q.q: If the law identifies no eligible relatives, where does the estate go, and how often does this happen?
o: To the Crown; rarely, because the recognized family trees are broad
To the court itself; very often, because most families are small
To the public trustee; rarely, because it requires a special claim
To charities; often, because executors usually prefer them
Q.e: If no eligible relatives exist, the estate passes to the Crown, meaning the provincial or territorial government. This is rare because the family trees recognized by law are broad, but it does happen when no one can be found.

Q.ti: Order of inheritance in an intestacy
Q.q: What is the broad intestacy pattern across common-law Canada when there is a spouse and children, and when there is no spouse?
o: The spouse takes everything, whatever the family; children inherit equally without a spouse
The children take everything and the spouse nothing; parents inherit without a spouse
The estate splits into equal thirds; siblings inherit if there is no spouse at all
Spouse and children share, usually after a preferential share; without a spouse, children inherit equally
Q.e: The surviving spouse is first in line. With children, the estate is shared, usually with a preferential share first. With no spouse, the children inherit equally, and then it moves outward to parents, siblings, and more distant relatives.

Q.q: Under the Ontario rules for deaths on or after March 1, 2021, a married spouse survives with two children, and the estate is $500,000. What does the spouse receive?
o: $400,000: the first $350,000 plus one-third of the remaining $150,000
$250,000: half of the whole estate under the preferential share rule
$350,000 only, with the children sharing the other $150,000
$500,000: the whole estate, since the spouse is first in line
Q.e: The spouse takes the first $350,000, leaving $150,000. With more than one child, the spouse takes one-third of that remainder ($50,000) and the children share the other two-thirds ($100,000), so the spouse receives $400,000 in all.

Q.ti: Intestacy in British Columbia and Alberta
Q.q: Which pairing matches the intestacy rules the chapter describes for British Columbia and Alberta?
o: BC: whole estate if all children are shared; Alberta: a $300,000 preferential share
BC: a $350,000 preferential share always; Alberta: one-third to the spouse
BC: $300,000 preferential share if all children are shared; Alberta: whole estate if shared
BC: nothing to a spouse ever; Alberta: $150,000 to the children only
Q.e: In BC the spouse receives a $300,000 preferential share when all children are also the spouse’s children, and $150,000 otherwise. In Alberta, if all children are shared with the spouse or adult interdependent partner, that person receives the entire estate.

Q.q: A married Quebec resident with children dies without a will. How is the estate divided, and is a liquidator still needed?
o: Two-thirds to the spouse, one-third to the children; no liquidator is needed
One-third to the spouse, two-thirds to the children; a liquidator is still needed
Half to the spouse and half to the children; the court acts as liquidator
The whole estate to the spouse; a liquidator is chosen by the notary
Q.e: Quebec’s Civil Code uses fixed fractions: with children, the spouse receives one-third and the children share two-thirds. Without a will, a liquidator is still needed to settle the estate, and the heirs usually choose one.

Q.ti: Using Appendix A and checking amounts
Q.q: Why does the chapter refer readers to Appendix A, and what warning does it give about preferential share amounts?
o: Rules are identical everywhere and amounts are fixed federally; no check is ever needed
Appendix A replaces legal advice, and amounts are set by each executor in turn
Appendix A lists only Ontario rules, and amounts are set by each family alone
Rules differ by province and amounts have changed; confirm with a lawyer or notary
Q.e: Appendix A sets out the rules for every province and territory side by side. Preferential share amounts have changed in the past and may change again, so check the current figure with a lawyer or notary before relying on it.

Q.q: How do Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta treat an unmarried partner in an intestacy?
o: Ontario: married spouses only; BC: two-year marriage-like partners; Alberta: adult interdependent partners
Ontario: partners after one year; BC: married spouses only; Alberta: married only
Ontario: adult interdependent partners; BC: ten-year partners only; Alberta: no partners
All three give unmarried partners no rights unless a will exists
Q.e: In BC, a marriage-like relationship of at least two years generally gives the same rights as a married spouse, and Alberta treats an adult interdependent partner the same. Ontario’s intestacy rules apply only to legally married spouses.

Q.ti: Options for common-law partners in Ontario
Q.q: An Ontario common-law partner who depended on the deceased finds no will. Which routes may help, and how does the chapter describe them?
o: Automatic inheritance after two years together; it counts as an inheritance
A claim under Quebec’s Civil Code; it counts as an inheritance
Nothing at all, because no route exists for unmarried partners there
A support claim and property outside the estate; neither is an inheritance
Q.e: A partner who was financially dependent may bring a dependant’s support claim and may receive property that passes outside the estate, such as a pension, life insurance, or a jointly held home. These are separate routes, not an inheritance.

Q.q: A married spouse in Ontario may choose between what the will or intestacy provides and another calculation. What is it, and how does the chapter describe the decision?
o: A flat share under the Succession Law Reform Act; an easy choice with no deadline
An equalization of net worth growth under the Family Law Act; a lawyer should advise
A share under the Dower Act; a decision made only by the executor
A claim under the Civil Code; a decision made only by a notary
Q.e: A surviving married spouse may be able to choose between the will or intestacy and a Family Law Act calculation that equalizes the growth in each spouse’s net worth. The deadline is short and the numbers are complex, so a lawyer should advise.

Q.q: What does Alberta’s Dower Act give a surviving married spouse?
o: Ownership of every asset the deceased held in any name at death
A life interest in the family home in some situations, whoever holds title
The right to override the will for any property over $150,000 in value
The right to be appointed executor of the estate automatically on death
Q.e: Alberta’s Dower Act gives a surviving married spouse a life interest in the family home in some situations, even where the deceased was the only person on title.

Q.q: How does the chapter describe de facto spouses in Quebec?
o: Heirs equal to married spouses in every case, with no reform needed at all
Heirs only after living together for two full years, in all provinces
Not heirs historically; a limited 2024 reform exists that a notary should confirm
Never heirs, and no reform of any kind has ever been proposed
Q.e: Spouses who are married or in a civil union are heirs, but de facto spouses long have not been. A 2024 reform creates a limited exception, which the chapter describes as reported, so a Quebec notary should confirm whether it applies.

Q.q: What can a family member ask a court to do under dependants’ relief or wills variation laws, and what principle underlies them?
o: Change how the estate is divided if provision is inadequate; freedom comes with obligations
Cancel the will completely; freedom to decide is absolute and cannot be limited
Replace the executor; freedom to decide belongs to the court alone
Delay probate for ten years; freedom to decide is shared by all relatives
Q.e: Every common-law province and territory lets certain family members ask a court to change how an estate is divided if the will or intestacy does not make adequate provision. Freedom to decide who receives your property comes with obligations to those who depended on you.

Q.ti: Ontario dependants and the claim deadline
Q.q: Under Ontario’s Succession Law Reform Act, who may qualify as a dependant, and when must a claim generally start?
o: Only legally married spouses; generally within two years of the death
A spouse, parent, child, or sibling being supported; generally within six months
Any friend of the deceased; generally within 180 days of the death
Only children under 18; generally within one year of the will
Q.e: A dependant includes a spouse, including a common-law spouse, a parent, a child, or a sibling whom the deceased was supporting just before death. A claim generally must start within six months of the grant of probate.

Q.q: Under Section 60 of British Columbia’s Wills, Estates and Succession Act, who may ask to vary a will, and what time limit generally applies?
o: A spouse or child, including adults; generally within 180 days of probate
Only a minor child; generally within six months of the death
Any heir named in the will; generally within two years of probate
Only a spouse who lived there; generally within 90 days of the death
Q.e: A spouse or a child of the deceased, including an adult child, may ask the court to vary the will if it does not make adequate, just, and equitable provision. A claim generally must be started within 180 days of the grant of probate.

Q.q: In Quebec, can a child be left out of a will, and who may claim a contribution from the estate?
o: No; every child must receive at least half of the intestacy share by law
Yes; but no one may claim a contribution from the estate afterward in court
Yes; a spouse, child, or parent owed support may claim within six months, with a cap
No; only a spouse may be left out, and only with a court’s approval
Q.e: Quebec protects testamentary freedom strongly, so a child can be left out. A spouse, child, or parent owed support can claim within six months, capped at half of the intestacy entitlement less what was received.

Q.q: If Priya dies without a will, who inherits, and what is the position of Chloe, Daniel’s daughter?
o: Arjun and Chloe inherit equally, because Priya helped raise both children
Daniel alone inherits; Arjun and Chloe have claims only as dependants
Maya inherits alone; Arjun and Chloe have no rights of any kind
Arjun inherits as her child; Chloe has none, since stepchildren are not heirs
Q.e: Arjun would inherit as Priya’s child, but Chloe would have no automatic rights, because stepchildren are not recognized as heirs. Whether Chloe could claim support depends on the province and the facts.

Q.q: How does a will contest differ from a support claim?
o: A support claim changes the will; a contest says the will should not count
A contest accepts the will and changes it; a support claim says it is invalid
Both rewrite the will, but only a contest has a time limit to meet
A contest is made by the executor; a support claim by beneficiaries
Q.e: A support claim accepts the will but asks the court to change what it provides. A contest argues that the will should not count at all, usually because the document itself is flawed.

Q.q: Which set lists the main grounds for challenging a will?
o: A large gift to charity, a gift to a pet, unequal shares, or a late signature
Signing or witnessing errors, lack of capacity, undue influence, and forgery or fraud
A change of mind, a move to a new province, a divorce, or a new baby
Handwriting that is hard to read, a short will, an old will, or a simple will
Q.e: A will may be challenged because it did not follow the formal rules of signing and witnessing, because the will-maker lacked testamentary capacity, because of undue influence, or because it was forged or obtained by fraud.

Q.ti: Suspicious circumstances and the burden of proof
Q.q: What suspicious circumstances do courts look at, and what can happen to the burden of proof when a challenger shows a real basis for suspicion?
o: A will with a large charity gift; the burden stays with the challenger
A will with many witnesses; the burden shifts to the court
A will with a typed signature; the burden shifts to the executor’s lawyer
A will favouring whoever arranged it; the burden can shift to its defender
Q.e: Courts look at a will favouring the person who arranged it, a sudden change shortly before death, or signing by someone frail and dependent. When a real basis for suspicion is shown, the burden can shift to the person defending the will.

Q.q: Who can bring a contest, and what time limits does the chapter mention?
o: Any stranger who is interested; ten years for capacity claims, longer for support
Only the executor; about 30 days for every kind of claim brought
A person with a real interest; around two years for capacity claims, shorter for support
Only a spouse; about five years for capacity, with support claims unlimited
Q.e: A challenger generally needs a real interest in the outcome, such as a family member or earlier beneficiary. Capacity or undue influence challenges are often limited to about two years, while support claims have much shorter deadlines.

Q.ti: Costs and prevention of will disputes
Q.q: What are the costs of estate litigation, and what does the chapter recommend as the best protection?
o: Quick and cheap but unfair to families; prevention, such as keeping the will secret
Paid by the estate in every case; prevention, such as naming many executors
Free for family members; prevention, such as signing a second will privately
Slow, costly, and hard on families; prevention, such as meeting the lawyer alone
Q.e: Estate litigation is slow and expensive, the losing side may pay part of the winner’s costs, and relationships can suffer. The best protection is prevention: meet the lawyer alone, record reasons for unusual choices, keep medical evidence, and tell the family.

Q.q: Margaret has a stroke and can no longer manage her money. Why would her will not help, and what would her children need?
o: It takes effect on incapacity; they would need only a bank’s own form
It covers only property abroad; they would need her doctor’s signed letter
It takes effect only at death; they would need to ask a court
It is revoked by incapacity; they would need a fresh will signed
Q.e: A will takes effect only at death, so it cannot help while Margaret is alive but incapable. Without a power of attorney, her children would have to ask a court to appoint a guardian, which a power of attorney is designed to avoid.

Q.ti: Authority to manage another adult’s property
Q.q: A husband’s house and investments are in his name alone, and his wife assumes being family is enough to manage them if he loses capacity. What does the chapter say?
o: Family status is enough for banks; joint accounts cover every asset he owns
Proof of authority is required; joint accounts do not cover sole-name property
A bank letter is enough for the house; joint accounts cover registered plans
A spouse may act freely; joint accounts also cover the house title
Q.e: Banks, pension plans, and government offices generally want written proof of authority. Joint accounts help for everyday banking, but they do not cover property held in one name, such as a house, a registered account, or an investment portfolio.

Q.ti: The two halves of incapacity planning
Q.q: Incapacity planning has two halves. Which pairing is correct?
o: Chapter 5 covers personal care; Chapter 6 covers property and finances
Chapter 5 covers wills; Chapter 6 covers funeral and burial plans
Chapter 5 covers court guardianship; Chapter 6 covers health insurance
Chapter 5 covers property and finances; Chapter 6 covers health and living decisions
Q.e: This chapter covers property and finances, and Chapter 6 covers personal care, meaning health and living decisions. Provinces handle them as separate documents with different names, and Pillar 2 is complete only when both are in place.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly lists causes of incapacity and what still happens while a person cannot manage affairs?
o: Dementia, retirement, a move, or long travel; bills and tax slips only
Stroke, divorce, inheritance, or a new job; rent and loan notices only
Dementia, stroke, accident, or long illness; bills and investments still need attention
Accident, marriage, a birth, or a windfall; bank statements and mail only
Q.e: Dementia, a stroke, a serious accident, or a long illness can leave a person unable to understand financial decisions. Meanwhile bills still arrive, rent or a mortgage must still be paid, and investments still need attention.

Q.q: Which statement about completing Pillar 2 of a plan is correct?
o: It needs both a property document and a personal care document
It needs a property document only, since a will covers care
It needs a personal care document only, since banks accept family
It needs a will and a funeral plan, since incapacity is rare
Q.e: Provinces treat property and personal care as separate documents with different names. Pillar 2 of the plan is complete only when both are in place, because a property document does not cover health decisions.

Q.q: What happens to a general power of attorney when the grantor loses capacity, and what is it suited for?
o: It ends; it suits a short, specific task such as closing a house sale
It continues; it suits ongoing care of a dependent adult for years
It ends; it suits managing a pension for the grantor’s whole life
It continues; it suits a short task such as closing a house sale
Q.e: A general power of attorney ends when you lose capacity, which is when it would be most useful, so it suits short, specific purposes such as closing a house sale. An enduring or continuing power keeps working after capacity is lost.

Q.q: Who is the “attorney” in a power of attorney, and what is the effect of that person’s acts?
o: A lawyer who drafts the document; their acts bind the lawyer’s firm
The person who witnesses the document; their acts bind no one outside court
The bank officer processing it; their acts bind the bank alone
The person authorized to act for you; their acts bind you legally
Q.e: In this context attorney does not mean a lawyer. It means the person you have authorized, who acts in your name, and what they do binds you legally.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly matches the document that keeps working after incapacity with the province?
o: Enduring in Ontario; continuing in British Columbia and Alberta
Protection mandate in Ontario; enduring power of attorney in Quebec
Continuing in Ontario; enduring in British Columbia and Alberta
Continuing power in Alberta; general power in British Columbia and Ontario
Q.e: Ontario uses continuing power of attorney for property, while British Columbia and Alberta use enduring power of attorney. Quebec uses a different instrument altogether, the protection mandate.

Q.q: Under Alberta’s guidance, how can an enduring power start, and who declares incapacity if the document names no one?
o: Only on a set date; one family member in a written note
Only on an event; the bank manager in a written note
On signing or death only; a judge in a written ruling
On signing, a set date, or an event; two medical practitioners in writing
Q.e: An enduring power can start on signing, on a set date, or on a specified event. If it depends on incapacity and names no one to declare it, two medical practitioners must make written declarations.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly describes the trade-offs of immediate and springing powers?
o: Immediate: slow for banks and safe; springing: fast and open to misuse
Immediate: easy for banks but open to misuse; springing: may cause delay
Immediate: needs a court order; springing: needs no proof of incapacity
Immediate: usable only after a declaration; springing: usable the day it is signed
Q.e: An immediate power is easy for banks to accept but gives authority while you are capable, creating a risk of misuse. A springing power is reassuring but can cause delays because proving incapacity may be unclear.

Q.q: What qualities should guide the choice of an attorney, and who can be named?
o: The eldest child, as birth order governs; only a relative can be named
The person who loves you most; only a lawyer can be named
Honest, organized, comfortable with money, and willing; a relative, friend, or professional
The closest neighbour; only a trust company can be named
Q.e: Choosing an attorney is a decision about trust, not love or birth order. The best choice is honest, organized, comfortable with money, and willing, and may be a relative, a friend, a trust company, or a professional.

Q.q: What is the benefit and risk of joint attorneys, and what alternative do some people use?
o: A check on each other but possible deadlock; one attorney for property, another for care
Faster decisions with no checks; the same attorney for property and for care
A check on each other with no risk of delay; one attorney only for property
No deadlock but weaker safeguards; two attorneys for care and none for property
Q.e: Joint attorneys add a check on each other but can deadlock. Some people therefore appoint one attorney for property and a different person to make care decisions.

Q.q: Why does the chapter say to name a backup attorney?
o: A backup is required by law in every province before the document is witnessed
Without an alternate, the document may fail if the first attorney dies or declines
A backup earns the first attorney a fee for any trouble caused
A backup removes the need for witnesses to sign the document
Q.e: If the first attorney dies, is unwell, or declines, and there is no alternate, the document may stop working at the very moment you need it. Alberta’s guidance lists this as one way an enduring power ends.

Q.q: What does an attorney owe the grantor?
o: A duty to claim a fee, mix funds for convenience, and report to the bank
A duty to follow the family’s wishes, share funds equally, and keep secrets
A duty to invest only in bonds, avoid all gifts, and report yearly to the court
A duty to act in the grantor’s interest, keep property separate, and keep records
Q.e: The attorney must act in the grantor’s interest, keep the grantor’s property separate from their own, and keep records. Rules about gifts, loans, and payment differ by province, so the document should say what you want.

Q.q: Which monitoring measures and warning signs does the chapter describe?
o: Annual court approval of each cheque; unusually low spending by the attorney
Monthly bank visits to the attorney; the attorney taking holidays
Statements to a second person; unexplained account changes and reluctance to share
Registration of every payment with the registry; polite behaviour by the attorney
Q.e: Monitoring is often missing from a plan. You can have statements sent to a second person or name a monitor. Warning signs include unexplained changes to accounts, reluctance to share information, and sudden, unusual spending.

Q.q: Which pairing describes the Quebec instrument used for incapacity, the people named, and what it can cover?
o: A general power of attorney; mandators; finances only in one document
An enduring directive; tutors; personal care only in a notarial form
A representation agreement; mandataries; finances only before two witnesses
A protection mandate; mandataries; personal care and finances in one document
Q.e: Quebec uses a protection mandate, also called a mandate in case of incapacity, naming one or more mandataries. A single document can cover both personal care and finances, made before a notary or before two witnesses.

Q.q: What is homologation, and what can the mandatary do before it?
o: Court approval after a declaration of incapacity; nothing, such as accessing bank accounts
Registration at the notary’s office on signing; pay bills but not sell property
A medical assessment alone; manage everything except real estate sales
Approval by the family; act freely while the person is incapable
Q.e: A protection mandate has no effect on the day of incapacity. The mandatary must apply to the Superior Court for a judgment declaring incapacity and homologating, meaning officially approving, the mandate. Until then the mandatary cannot, for example, access bank accounts.

Q.q: What does a homologation application need, and how long does the process take?
o: The mandate, a family letter, and a bank statement; a few days in all
The mandate, medical and psychosocial assessments, and register searches; several months
A will, a medical letter, and two witnesses; about one or two weeks
A tax return, a lawyer’s opinion, and register searches; about one month
Q.e: The application needs the original mandate or certified copy, a medical assessment, a psychosocial assessment, and register search certificates. A 2020 guide estimated several months to gather documents and another three to six months for the procedure.

Q.q: After the judgment, who records the details, and what may happen if the court cannot homologate the mandate?
o: The Curateur public records them in a register; a tutorship may follow
The notary records them in the will register; a liquidator may follow
The Superior Court records them in a tax file; a general power may follow
The bank records them in its customer file; accounts may be frozen
Q.e: The Curateur public records the details in the public register of homologated mandates. If the court cannot homologate, for example because the mandatary cannot perform the role and no substitute is named, it may establish a tutorship instead.

Q.q: Can an ordinary power of attorney replace a protection mandate in Quebec, and why?
o: Yes; it continues after incapacity in Quebec just as elsewhere
Yes; it is approved automatically by the Superior Court on request
No; it stops being valid when the person becomes incapacitated
No; it can be used only with the notary’s original in hand
Q.e: Some Quebecers use an ordinary power of attorney, but it stops being valid when the person becomes incapacitated, so it cannot replace a protection mandate.

Q.q: When a person is already incapable and has no valid power of attorney, what is the only route, and what do guardianship, trusteeship, and tutorship show?
o: The bank; different names for three unrelated private documents
A court; each name describes a judge appointing someone to manage
A notary; the same name used in every province and territory
The public trustee; different names for a power signed in advance
Q.e: When no valid power of attorney exists, the only route is a court. The names differ, including guardianship of property in Ontario, trusteeship in Alberta, and tutorship or curatorship in Quebec, but a judge appoints someone to manage the affairs.

Q.q: In Ontario, who can apply for guardianship of property, and what must the application include?
o: Only the spouse; a will and a certified copy of the marriage record
Only a lawyer; a signed power of attorney and a bank statement
Any bank; a letter from the family doctor and a tax return
Anyone; a management plan explaining how the property will be handled
Q.e: In Ontario, anyone can apply to the Superior Court of Justice to be guardian of property, and the application must include a management plan explaining how the property will be handled.

Q.q: What are the disadvantages of guardianship compared with a power of attorney?
o: Slower, costlier, and public; the court may require reports or a bond
Faster and cheaper but public; the court may require reports or a bond
Slower but private; the appointee is always the person the individual would pick
Costlier but private; the court requires nothing from the person appointed
Q.e: Guardianship is slower, costs more, and makes private family finances a matter of public court records. The court may require reports, an accounting, or a bond, and the person appointed may not be the one the incapable person would have chosen.

Q.q: In Alberta, who may need to go to court to become a person’s trustee, and what does the province’s guidance say about the process?
o: Only a public official; it is quick and inexpensive for families
Only a lawyer; it is automatic once a doctor writes a letter
Only a spouse; it needs no court application at all
A family member or friend; it takes time and money
Q.e: In Alberta, a family member or friend may need to go to court to become the person’s trustee, which, as the province’s guidance says, takes time and money.

Q.q: What solution does the chapter suggest for Margaret, and how does it compare the costs?
o: A will naming both children; hours with a lawyer versus years in tax court
A power of attorney naming both children; hours with a lawyer versus months in court
A guardianship application filed early; a day with a clerk versus a small fee
A joint bank account with one child; a form versus a lengthy hearing
Q.e: A power of attorney naming her daughter and son as joint attorneys, or naming one with the other as backup, would avoid guardianship. The cost today is a few hours with a lawyer, while having nothing may mean months of court process.

Q.ti: Consent and the right to refuse treatment
Q.q: What right does a capable adult have in health care, and what do professionals generally need?
o: To accept treatment but not refuse it; a court order before they treat
To refuse treatment only in hospital; a spouse’s consent before they treat
To accept or refuse treatment; informed consent before they treat
To name a treatment; a pharmacist’s approval before they treat
Q.e: A capable adult has the right to accept or refuse medical treatment, and health professionals generally need informed consent before they treat. That right belongs to you for as long as you have capacity.

Q.q: Capacity is presumed. How is it judged, and what does Quebec’s guidance add?
o: Once for life, and it never changes; a doctor checks it yearly
Decision by decision, and it can change; professionals check it each time
Only by a court, and it cannot change; a notary checks it
By diagnosis alone, and it can change; a nurse checks it yearly
Q.e: Capacity is presumed, judged for each decision, and can change with time or with the kind of decision. Quebec’s guidance says every person is presumed capable of consenting to care, and the professional must check capacity each time care is offered.

Q.q: When capacity is lost, what happens to the right to consent, and what is the person who exercises it called?
o: It disappears; the doctor alone decides, acting as an attending guardian
It does not disappear; someone else exercises it, called a substitute decision-maker
It passes to the family; the person is called a care trustee
It is suspended until recovery; the court calls the person a monitor
Q.e: When capacity is lost, the right to consent does not disappear, but someone else must exercise it. That person is called a substitute decision-maker, a term used across the country.

Q.ti: The default list and the risk of guessing
Q.q: Without planning, who picks the substitute decision-maker, and what risk follows?
o: The law, from a fixed list; the doctor may not know your wishes
The hospital board, by vote; the family may argue about the vote
The eldest child, by right; the other children may be excluded
The doctor, from personal preference; the hospital may overrule the choice
Q.e: Without planning, the law picks the person for you from a fixed list, and the doctor may not know what you would have wanted.

Q.q: After a serious fall, Margaret has named no one to decide. What problem arises for her children?
o: They would need a will, which takes effect at incapacity
The Hamilton hospital would refuse to ask either child for consent
Her son would automatically outrank her daughter by birth order
They are equally ranked, live far apart, and may disagree about surgery
Q.e: Margaret’s son and daughter are equally ranked in the law, live far apart, and may disagree. A short document and one honest conversation years earlier could have spared them that.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly matches provinces with their personal care documents?
o: Ontario: personal directive; BC: power of attorney; Alberta: representation agreement
Ontario: representation agreement; BC: personal directive; Alberta: protection mandate
Ontario: protection mandate; BC: continuing power; Alberta: advance directive only
Ontario: attorney for personal care; BC: representation agreement; Alberta: personal directive
Q.e: Ontario uses a power of attorney for personal care, naming an attorney for personal care. British Columbia uses a representation agreement, and Alberta uses a personal directive, in which you may name an agent.

Q.q: In Quebec, which two instruments cover personal care planning?
o: A personal directive for treatment, and a representation agreement to name a person
A health care proxy for treatment, and a continuing power to name a person
Advance medical directives for treatment, and the protection mandate to name a person
An advance directive for tutors, and a will to name a person
Q.e: Quebec uses advance medical directives for specific treatment choices and the protection mandate, covered in Chapter 5, to name someone to look after your person.

Q.ti: Eligibility in British Columbia and Alberta
Q.q: Which pairing about age and capacity to make a personal care document is correct?
o: BC: 19 or older and capable; Alberta: any capable person 18 or older
BC: 18 or older and capable; Alberta: 19 or older, with a lawyer
BC: 19 or older; Alberta: any age if a parent consents
BC: any capable adult; Alberta: 21 or older and a resident
Q.e: In British Columbia you must be 19 or older and capable to make a section 9 representation agreement, and your representative must also be 19 or older. Alberta allows any capable person aged 18 or older to make a personal directive.

Q.q: How does a British Columbia section 7 representation agreement differ from a section 9 agreement?
o: Section 7 is fuller and needs two lawyers as witnesses
Section 7 is more limited, for adults who already have some incapacity
Section 9 is limited and is for minors only
Section 9 is for adults who already lack all capacity
Q.e: British Columbia also has a more limited section 7 representation agreement for adults who already have some incapacity and cannot make the fuller section 9 type.

Q.q: Which pairing of witnessing rules is described in the chapter?
o: Alberta: no witness needed; BC section 9: two witnesses, or one lawyer or notary
Alberta: the agent’s spouse; BC section 9: one friend of the maker
Alberta: two witnesses, one a physician; BC section 9: a court clerk
Alberta: one qualified witness; BC section 9: two witnesses, or one lawyer or notary
Q.e: In Alberta, a personal directive must be dated and signed in front of a witness, who cannot be the agent, the agent’s partner, or the maker’s partner. A BC section 9 agreement needs two witnesses, or one if a lawyer or notary.

Q.q: In Ontario, how does the list under the Health Care Consent Act begin, and who steps in when equally ranked people disagree?
o: The spouse, then the eldest child; the Consent and Capacity Board
A guardian, then a named attorney; the Public Guardian and Trustee
A close friend, then the family doctor; the hospital ethics committee
The eldest relative, then a parent; the Superior Court automatically
Q.e: Ontario’s list begins with a court-appointed guardian of the person, then an attorney for personal care, then a board-appointed representative, spouse, child or parent, sibling, and other relatives. The Public Guardian and Trustee decides when equals disagree.

Q.ti: Naming someone to the top of the list
Q.q: What lets someone lower on Ontario’s list move to the top?
o: Naming them in a personal care document
Living closest to the hospital, regardless of any document
Being the eldest child, regardless of any document
Paying the hospital bills, regardless of any document
Q.e: Ontario’s list shows the key point: you can lift anyone from lower on the list to the top by naming them in a document.

Q.q: In British Columbia, with no representative or directive, who chooses a temporary substitute, and who qualifies first?
o: The Public Guardian and Trustee; the eldest child, if willing
A court; the closest friend, if present at the hospital
The patient’s lawyer; the parent, if over sixty-five years old
A health care provider; the spouse, including a common-law spouse, if qualified
Q.e: A health care provider chooses a temporary substitute from a list, and the first person who qualifies is chosen, starting with the spouse, including a common-law spouse, then child, parent, sibling, and so on.

Q.q: Which qualifications must a British Columbia temporary substitute meet?
o: 19 or older, willing, capable, available, no dispute with you, and recent contact
18 or older, willing, a relative, available, no dispute with you, and contact within a decade
19 or older, a lawyer, capable, available, and living in the same city
19 or older, willing, capable, and living within fifty kilometres
Q.e: To qualify, the person must be 19 or older, willing, capable, and available, have no dispute with you, and have been in contact with you in the past year.

Q.q: In Quebec, who consents for an incapable person with a homologated mandate, with a private tutorship, and with no representation?
o: The notary; the court; the Curateur public, then a close friend
The tutor; the mandatary; the eldest child, then the Curateur public
The mandatary; the tutor; the spouse, then a close relative
The spouse; the notary; the Curateur public, then a close relative
Q.e: With a homologated protection mandate it is the mandatary, under a private tutorship it is the tutor, and with no representation it is the spouse, then a close relative, then a person with a special interest. The Curateur public acts only as a last resort.

Q.q: Which qualities make a good personal care decision-maker, according to the chapter?
o: Loves you most, lives next door, and agrees with every choice
Is the eldest child, lives nearby, and agrees with every doctor
Is a lawyer, lives abroad, and decides by personal preference
Stays calm, understands your values, speaks to doctors, and follows your wishes
Q.e: The best decision-maker is rarely the person who loves you most. It is someone who can stay calm in a hospital corridor, understand what you value, speak up to doctors, and act on your wishes even when they would choose differently.

Q.ti: Asking first and the risk of deadlock
Q.q: Why should you ask before naming someone, and what risk does Alberta’s guidance mention for several agents?
o: They can decline while you can still choose; joint agents may deadlock
The law requires their signature first; separate agents can never deadlock
It saves a witness; several agents each hold a veto over doctors
It lowers hospital fees; several agents must always be an odd number
Q.e: A person who has agreed in advance knows the role and can say no while you can still choose someone else. Alberta warns that several agents act jointly unless the directive says otherwise, and an even number can lead to deadlock.

Q.q: In what order is a decision-maker guided?
o: Your best interests, your instructions, your family’s views, then your doctor’s opinion
Your instructions, then what you said, then your values, then your best interests
Your family’s views, your instructions, your doctor’s opinion, then your values
Your values, your best interests, your instructions, then what you said
Q.e: A decision-maker is guided first by any instructions you left, then by what you said when you were capable, then by your known values and beliefs, and finally by your best interests. The more they know, the less they guess.

Q.q: Which are examples of instructions tied to real situations?
o: Life support if recovery is unlikely, artificial nutrition, and moving into long-term care
Favourite hospital meals, preferred television, and the visiting schedule
Choice of hospital pharmacy, parking, and the ward’s visiting hours
Which relative signs the bill, who parks, and the visiting schedule
Q.e: Specific instructions help most when tied to real situations, such as life support if recovery is unlikely, artificial nutrition, or moving into long-term care. Values are just as useful, such as wanting to be at home.

Q.q: According to British Columbia’s guidance, what can a representative not do unless the agreement clearly allows it?
o: Consent to routine surgery, ordinary tests, or standard medication
Choose the family doctor or the hospital for ordinary care
Request medical assistance in dying or consent to research, sterilization, or donation
Speak with doctors about the person’s wishes and values
Q.e: A representative cannot request medical assistance in dying, and cannot consent to treatments that are not medically necessary, such as research, sterilization, or organ or tissue donation, unless the agreement clearly allows it.

Q.q: Who should receive copies of a personal care document, and what does a registry such as Alberta’s hold?
o: Only the lawyer who drafted it; the registry holds a full copy
Decision-maker, backup, doctor, relative; the registry may hold no copy
The bank and the notary; the registry holds a certified copy
Only the decision-maker; the registry replaces any other copies
Q.e: Give a copy to your decision-maker, your backup, your family doctor, and a trusted relative. A registry usually records only that a document exists, and Alberta’s optional registry does not hold a copy of the directive.

Q.q: When does an Alberta personal directive take effect, and who must be notified?
o: On signing; the doctor notifies the court within thirty days of signing
After a court order; the registry notifies the whole family afterward
After incapacity is declared; the agent notifies the nearest relative and legal representative
On the maker’s death; the executor then notifies the nearest relative
Q.e: Alberta’s personal directive takes effect after you are declared incapable of making personal decisions. The agent must then notify the nearest relative and the maker’s legal representative.

Q.q: Under Alberta’s approach, what follows if a person declared incapable later recovers?
o: Capacity can be reassessed, and decision-making authority returns to the maker
The agent keeps authority until the directive expires in ten years
The directive is cancelled and must be signed again before a witness
The agent keeps authority only over long-term care decisions
Q.e: Capacity can be reassessed, so if you recover, your decision-making authority returns. The directive takes effect after incapacity is declared and does not remove the maker’s rights permanently.

Q.q: A family disagrees about a patient’s care. What first steps does the chapter suggest, and what review body exists in Ontario?
o: Go straight to court; the Public Guardian and Trustee’s tribunal
Ask the bank to intervene; the hospital’s billing office
Keep records and meet the care team; the Consent and Capacity Board
Ask the lawyer to withdraw; the Superior Court’s family branch
Q.e: Disagreements usually arise when people did not know what you wanted. Keep records, ask for a meeting with the care team, and seek ethics or patient-relations support before turning to courts. In Ontario the Consent and Capacity Board can review disagreements.

Q.q: When should a personal care document be reviewed, and how should a replacement be handled?
o: Only every twenty years; leave the old copies with everyone
Only after a death; destroy the new version and keep the old
Only at the hospital’s request; give the new version to the bank
After events like divorce or a move; give every copy holder the new version
Q.e: Review every few years and after big events such as a divorce, the death of a decision-maker, a new diagnosis, or a move. Revoke by signing a new document, and make sure everyone holding a copy receives the new version.

Q.ti: Advance care planning as a process
Q.q: What does advance care planning involve, and how do the Chapter 6 documents relate to it?
o: A single form signed once; the documents are the whole of it
A court procedure for incapable adults; the documents are filed with it
A medical test for older adults; the documents are optional extras
A process of reflection and communication; the documents are one result, not the whole
Q.e: Advance care planning is a process of reflection and communication, not a single form. It involves thinking about what matters, learning about illness and treatment, choosing a decision-maker, talking, and recording. The Chapter 6 documents are one result of it.

Q.ti: The five steps of advance care planning
Q.q: Which sequence lists the five steps in the Speak Up approach, and which step is optional?
o: Think, learn, decide, talk, record; writing it down is optional
Learn, record, think, decide, sign; talking is optional
Think, record, witness, file, decide; deciding is optional
Talk, sign, file, learn, decide; thinking is optional
Q.e: The national Speak Up campaign describes five steps: think, learn, decide, talk, and record. Recording means writing your wishes down, which is optional, and the written plan may be called an advance directive or medical directive.

Q.q: When does a written plan matter, and how often may it change?
o: From the day it is signed; it can change only with a court’s approval
Only if you cannot decide; it can change often if the decision-maker has the latest copy
Only after a hospital admission; it can change once a year at most, by a doctor
Only after age 65; it can change only when the family doctor agrees
Q.e: A written plan matters only if you cannot make your own health care decisions, and until then your own consent counts. It can be changed as often as you like, as long as your decision-maker has a copy of your latest wishes.

Q.q: In Quebec, what must a substitute do when a person wrote an advance medical directive while capable?
o: Ignore it, because only a court may apply a directive of this kind
Follow it only if the substitute agrees with each instruction in it
Follow it only if a notary registered it before the illness began
Follow it, even if the substitute disagrees, when the physician considers the care necessary
Q.e: Quebec’s advance medical directives form lets you state wishes about specific treatments. Provincial guidance says the substitute must follow a directive written while capable, even if the substitute disagrees, when the physician considers the care necessary.

Q.q: Margaret avoids the subject because it feels morbid, yet her daughter wants to know her wishes. What does the chapter say such a conversation often does?
o: Raises fears too early and increases conflict between relatives
Commits the person to treatment choices that cannot be changed
Relieves both sides by replacing guessing with understanding
Removes the need for any later written plan or discussion
Q.e: The conversation often turns out to be relieving for both sides, since it replaces guessing with understanding. A conversation held in good health is easier than one held in a hospital corridor.

Q.q: How does the chapter suggest starting the conversation, and why start there?
o: With medical terms first; they replace the need for any later conversation
With the funeral plan; it avoids questions about care and costs
With values, not medical terms; they help a decision-maker answer new questions
With a lawyer’s form; it settles every future question the family raises
Q.e: The chapter suggests beginning with values: what a good day looks like, what you fear, and what must be present for life to feel worthwhile. These questions give a decision-maker a way to answer questions no document anticipated.

Q.q: Which medical questions does the chapter suggest thinking about, and who can explain them?
o: Hospital food, parking, and visiting hours; the hospital pharmacist on duty
CPR, breathing machines, feeding, dialysis, and care homes; the family doctor
Tax rates, wills, and probate fees; the family lawyer in town
Insurance premiums, pensions, and loans; the bank adviser at the branch
Q.e: Consider CPR, a breathing machine, artificial feeding, dialysis, or moving to a care home. Your family doctor or nurse practitioner can explain what each treatment involves and how likely it is to help, which makes your wishes more reliable.

Q.q: How does a written plan differ from a medical order?
o: A plan is written by a doctor; an order records what the patient wants
A plan binds first responders; an order is written by a family lawyer
A plan is a court order; an order is written by a notary public
A plan records your wishes; an order is written by a doctor or nurse
Q.e: Your written plan records what you want. A medical order is an instruction written by a doctor or nurse practitioner that health teams and first responders follow.

Q.q: Which pairing of provincial medical orders is described in the chapter?
o: Alberta: Goals of Care Designation; BC: No CPR Form with two signatures
Alberta: No CPR Form; BC: Goals of Care Designation signed by a notary public
Alberta: MOST only; BC: advance directive signed by one witness and a lawyer
Alberta: representation agreement; BC: personal directive signed by two witnesses
Q.e: In Alberta a Goals of Care Designation is a medical order written by a doctor or nurse practitioner. In British Columbia a No CPR Form must be signed by both the adult and a physician or nurse practitioner.

Q.q: Can a No CPR order be cancelled, and does it mean no care?
o: No, once signed; it ends every treatment except pain relief
Yes, but only by a court; it ends all hospital care
No, it is permanent; it ends antibiotics and dialysis
Yes, at any time; pain, antibiotics, dialysis, and nutrition support can continue
Q.e: Orders of this kind can be cancelled at any time, even after signing. A No CPR order does not mean no care, since people can still receive pain and symptom management, antibiotics, dialysis, and nutritional support.

Q.q: What is palliative care, and when can it begin?
o: Care only in the last days of life; it starts when all treatment stops
A form of treatment meant to cure; it is given at diagnosis only
Comfort-focused care for life-limiting illness; it can begin well before the end
Care given only in a hospice residence; it starts on admission day
Q.e: Palliative care focuses on quality of life for people with a progressive, life-limiting illness, including pain management and emotional, social, and spiritual support. It can be given alongside treatments that slow or cure the illness and can begin well before the end.

Q.q: Who benefits most from palliative support, and what should a person with a serious illness do?
o: Advanced-illness patients who ask early; ask the doctor about a palliative approach
Only people in their final days; wait quietly until it is offered
Only people without family support; wait for a hospice referral
Only young patients; ask the pharmacist about a palliative approach
Q.e: Those who benefit most are often the ones who ask late. Someone with advanced heart failure, lung disease, or cancer may live for months or years with palliative support, so it is reasonable to ask the doctor rather than wait to be offered it.

Q.q: Where can palliative care be provided, and what shapes the services available?
o: Only in hospital; it depends on the patient’s age and income level
Home, hospital, long-term care, or hospice; depends on province, community, and funding
Only at home; it depends on the family’s wishes and insurance plan
Only in hospice residences; it depends on the hospital’s size and staffing
Q.e: Palliative care can be provided at home, in a hospital, in a long-term care home, or in a hospice residence. Services depend on your province, your community, and the funding behind them, and rural, remote, and northern communities are often hardest to serve.

Q.q: Which pairing of terms is correct?
o: Palliative care is the approach; hospice is a service or place
Palliative care is a place; hospice is the broad approach
Hospice means end-of-life care only; palliative care means a nursing home
Palliative care means MAID; hospice means the final week only
Q.e: Palliative care is the broad approach, and hospice is a type of service or a place. End-of-life care refers to care in the final period of life.

Q.q: Is a person who asks about MAID still entitled to palliative support, and how does the chapter treat the two?
o: No; asking about MAID ends access to palliative support
Yes; but only if the person first declines MAID
No; palliative care and MAID are the same service under different names
Yes; MAID is a separate matter that some consider alongside palliative care
Q.e: Medical assistance in dying is a separate matter that some people consider alongside palliative care, and a person who requests it can also receive palliative support.

Q.q: What is a hospice, and how does it differ from a nursing home?
o: A nursing home for long stays; it ends all medical treatment
A comfort-focused place or program; it is not a nursing home
A hospital ward for surgery; it replaces palliative care entirely
A funeral service for families; it begins after death
Q.e: A hospice is a place or program providing comfort-focused care at the end of life. It is not the same as a nursing home, and it is not a place where treatment stops. It is a setting built around comfort and dignity.

Q.q: What does a hospice often offer besides residential care?
o: Legal drafting, will storage, and probate filing for families
Surgery, rehabilitation, and diagnostic testing for patients
Day programs, home visiting, and bereavement support for families
Tax filing, pension transfers, and insurance claims for families
Q.e: Residential hospices provide round-the-clock care, usually in the final weeks or months, and many also run day programs, home visiting, and bereavement support for families.

Q.q: Which statement about hospice costs is consistent with the chapter?
o: Plans usually cover inpatient hospice care; home medicines and equipment may not be
Plans never cover hospice care, so every cost is private to the family
Plans cover everything at home, with unlimited nursing hours for all
Residents pay nothing in long-term care, and hospice costs are identical everywhere
Q.e: According to the chapter, provincial plans usually cover hospital inpatient hospice care, but home-based care may not cover medicines and equipment and some plans limit covered hours. Private insurance, personal funds, and community agencies can fill gaps.

Q.q: How does hospice bed supply compare with best practice, and what follows?
o: About 7 per 100,000 against about four; empty beds and short waits
About 3.97 per 1,000 against about seven; no effect on access
About 3.97 per 100,000 against about seven; waiting lists and long distances
About 20 per 100,000 against about ten; shorter lists nearly everywhere
Q.e: The Canadian Cancer Society reports best practice is about seven hospice beds per 100,000 people, while Canada averages about 3.97. In practice that means waiting lists, long distances, and many people ending up in a hospital or at home with less support.

Q.q: What does dying at home usually require?
o: A funeral plan, a will, an executor on call, and a hospice reference
A capable caregiver, home nursing, equipment, an emergency plan, and an agreed backup
Only a family doctor’s promise and a hospice bed reserved in advance
Only a willing neighbour and a one-time visit by a nurse
Q.e: Many people want to die at home and many manage it with enough help. That usually requires a capable caregiver, home care nursing, equipment such as a hospital bed, a plan for emergencies, and an agreed backup, such as a hospice bed.

Q.q: Planning for the caregiver is part of planning for the patient. What can it include?
o: A funeral plan, a will, a probate application, and a gravesite
A second home, a loan, a guardianship order, and a new vehicle
Time off work, income support, respite, and a backup caregiver
A tax return, a court bond, and a hospice waiting list entry
Q.e: Caring for a seriously ill person is demanding and often falls to one family member. Planning for the caregiver can include time off work, income support, respite, and a plan for who steps in when the main caregiver is exhausted.

Q.q: Which pairing of Employment Insurance caregiving benefits and maximum weeks is correct?
o: Compassionate care: 15; adults: 35; children: 26
Compassionate care: 35; adults: 26; children: 15
Compassionate care: 26; adults: 15; children: 35
Compassionate care: 52; adults: 15; children: 26
Q.e: The compassionate care benefit provides up to 26 weeks, the family caregiver benefit for adults up to 15 weeks, and the benefit for children up to 35 weeks. The weeks can be shared among eligible caregivers.

Q.q: Who counts as a caregiver for these benefits, and who certifies the patient’s condition?
o: Only blood relatives who live together; a lawyer
Only spouses and parents living in the same home; a notary public
Only adult children; the employer’s payroll office
Anyone treated like family; a doctor or nurse practitioner
Q.e: The caregiver does not have to live with the person or be related by blood or marriage, since the rules treat as family anyone considered like family. The condition must be certified by a medical doctor or nurse practitioner.

Q.q: For end-of-life care benefits, what must the certificate state, and what else should caregivers check?
