o: A diagnosis of terminal cancer; the hospital’s rules about family visiting
Risk of death within 26 weeks; provincial labour law on job protection
A hospice admission date; the bank’s rules about lending to caregivers
A risk of death within five years; the municipal rules on property tax
Q.e: For end-of-life care the certificate must state a significant risk of death within 26 weeks. Employment protection depends on provincial and territorial labour law, so caregivers should check both before leaving work.

Q.q: Which supports do families often need that no benefit pays for?
o: Respite care, counselling, support groups, and bereavement services
Probate fees, will drafting, and court filings
Mortgage relief, pension credits, and tax refunds
Equipment loans, bonds, and court filing fees
Q.e: Respite care gives the family caregiver a break, and counselling, support groups, and bereavement services are available through hospices and community organizations. Families do better when they ask early rather than waiting for a crisis.

Q.ti: Definition and legal basis of MAID
Q.q: What is MAID, and which law governs it?
o: A hospital policy at a family’s request; provincial health acts and hospital by-laws
A tax benefit at a doctor’s request; the Income Tax Act and its regulations
A court remedy at a spouse’s request; the Civil Code of Québec and local rules
A lawful medical service at a capable adult’s voluntary request; the federal Criminal Code
Q.e: MAID is a lawful medical service in which a physician or nurse practitioner, at a capable adult’s voluntary request, provides or prescribes medication that causes death. The federal Criminal Code sets the national rules and safeguards.

Q.q: Who organizes delivery of MAID, and what is the position of practitioners who object?
o: Parliament; every practitioner must provide it when a patient requests it
Hospitals only; objecting practitioners must refer the matter to a court of law
Provinces and territories; no practitioner must provide it, but systems connect willing ones
Municipal boards; objecting practitioners must step down from practising medicine
Q.e: Provinces and territories organize delivery, which is why experience differs. The law does not require any individual practitioner to provide MAID, although health systems must have ways to connect patients with willing providers.

Q.ti: MAID compared with other end-of-life decisions
Q.q: Which of the following is MAID, rather than another end-of-life decision?
o: Giving medication under the law at the person’s request to cause death
Refusing or stopping a treatment that a capable person no longer wants
Receiving palliative care to relieve pain and other symptoms of illness
Signing a No CPR order that refuses resuscitation if the heart stops
Q.e: Refusing or stopping treatment, palliative care, and a No CPR order are not MAID. In MAID the cause of death is the medication provided under the law, which is why it is surrounded by specific safeguards.

Q.q: Which statement matches Health Canada’s 2024 figures as given in the chapter?
o: 16,499 provisions, about 15 percent of deaths; Ontario had the largest share
16,499 provisions, about 5.1 percent of deaths; Quebec had the largest share
1,649 provisions, about 5.1 percent of deaths; Quebec had the smallest share
16,499 provisions, about 0.5 percent of deaths; British Columbia had the largest share
Q.e: Health Canada’s 2024 report records 16,499 provisions, about 5.1 percent of all deaths. Quebec accounted for 36.4 percent, Ontario 30.0 percent, and British Columbia 18.2 percent.

Q.q: Can a power of attorney or a personal directive authorize MAID, and what does MAID depend on?
o: In general no; it needs your own capable, voluntary request and consent
Yes; the attorney’s signature can replace the person’s own request
Yes; but only with letters from two physicians supporting the request
No; it depends on a court order and a family vote
Q.e: In general a personal directive, a representation agreement, or a power of attorney cannot authorize MAID. It depends on your own capable, voluntary request and final consent, with only narrow exceptions.

Q.q: Which set of conditions describes eligibility under federal law?
o: Be 16 or older, with any chronic illness, and a request signed by family
Be 18 or older, with a terminal diagnosis only, and a lawyer’s approval
Be an adult with capacity, a grievous and irremediable condition, and a voluntary request
Be any age with a capable parent, a serious illness, and a spouse’s request
Q.e: You must live in Canada and be eligible for government-funded health services, be at least 18 and capable, have a grievous and irremediable condition, and make a voluntary request free of outside pressure, with informed consent.

Q.q: What does a grievous and irremediable condition mean?
o: Any illness that a doctor finds inconvenient or costly to treat at home
A temporary illness that causes occasional discomfort but later improves
Any condition that is covered by provincial health insurance plans
A serious illness or disability in irreversible decline causing unbearable suffering
Q.e: The condition is a serious illness, disease, or disability in an advanced state of decline that cannot be reversed, causing unbearable suffering that cannot be relieved in ways you consider acceptable.

Q.q: Which pairing describes the two pathways and their share of 2024 provisions?
o: Foreseeable death, about 95.6 percent; not foreseeable, about 4.4 percent with more safeguards
Not foreseeable, about 95.6 percent; foreseeable death, about 4.4 percent with more safeguards
Foreseeable death, about 50 percent; not foreseeable, about 50 percent with no extra safeguards
Foreseeable death, about 70 percent; not foreseeable, about 30 percent with a court hearing
Q.e: In the first pathway natural death is reasonably foreseeable, which accounted for about 95.6 percent of 2024 provisions. In the second it is not, about 4.4 percent, and the law adds extra safeguards.

Q.ti: Mental illness as a sole condition
Q.q: At the time of writing, what is the position of a person whose only condition is mental illness, and what should readers do?
o: Eligible now, because the exclusion ended in March 2027
Eligible only in Quebec; the exclusion applies elsewhere forever
Not currently eligible; confirm the current text of the law
Not eligible, and the law is certain and will never be reviewed
Q.e: A person whose only underlying condition is mental illness is not currently eligible. The government announced in October 2026 that the exclusion will continue indefinitely, but legislation had not been tabled, so readers should confirm the current law.

Q.q: Can a person withdraw a MAID request, and does eligibility last?
o: Only before the written request is signed; eligibility is then permanent
Yes, up to the final moment; a request is not a commitment
Only with a physician’s written permission; eligibility ends at withdrawal
No, once it is approved; eligibility is final for the person
Q.e: Eligibility is not permanent. You can be eligible and later change your mind, and you can withdraw your request at any time, up to the final moment. A request is not a commitment.

Q.q: How does the process begin, and who may witness the request?
o: A verbal request; any family member who is at least 16 years old
A court application; the person’s treating physician or nurse practitioner
A physician’s referral; an unpaid caregiver who lives with the person
A signed written request; an independent witness who cannot benefit
Q.e: The process begins with a written request signed and dated before one independent witness who is at least 18, cannot benefit from the person’s death, cannot be an unpaid caregiver, and cannot own or operate the facility where the person is cared for.

Q.q: Who assesses the request, and who may provide MAID?
o: One practitioner; physicians and pharmacists in every province and territory
Two independent practitioners; physicians, plus nurse practitioners where permitted
Two family members; physicians and registered nurses working in any setting
A hospital committee; physicians and social workers where a province permits it
Q.e: Two independent practitioners assess the request, and the second must give a written opinion confirming eligibility. Only physicians, and nurse practitioners where a province permits it, can conduct assessments and provide MAID.

Q.q: What extra safeguards apply when natural death is not reasonably foreseeable?
o: Expert input, options discussed, and an assessment lasting at least 90 days
A court hearing, a family vote, and an assessment of one week
A second witness, a clergy letter, and an assessment of one year
A tribunal review, a spouse’s consent, and an assessment of 30 days
Q.e: One assessor must have expertise in the condition, or a consultation must occur. The person must be told about ways to relieve suffering, and the assessment must take at least 90 days, unless the person is at immediate risk of losing capacity.

Q.q: What must happen immediately before MAID is provided, and what is a waiver of final consent?
o: The family signs again; an exception for any person who loses capacity
A judge confirms consent; an exception when death is not foreseeable
Consent is confirmed; a narrow waiver exists when death is foreseeable
A pharmacist verifies identity; an exception exists for patients under 18
Q.e: Immediately before MAID the person must be offered the chance to withdraw and must confirm consent. A waiver of final consent exists only if natural death is reasonably foreseeable and specific conditions were met while the person had capacity.

Q.q: In Quebec, what is the provincial term, and what applies if natural death is not reasonably foreseeable?
o: Medical aid in dying; a third specialist opinion and 90 days may be needed
Medical assistance in death; a fourth opinion and a 30-day wait are needed
Assisted care at end of life; a court order and 180 days are needed
Medical aid in dying; no second opinion is ever needed in any case
Q.e: Quebec has its own Act respecting end-of-life care, and its term is medical aid in dying. If natural death is not reasonably foreseeable, a third opinion from a specialist may be needed and at least 90 days must pass.

Q.ti: Capacity at the time of MAID
Q.q: Under federal law at the time of writing, must a person be capable when MAID is provided, and what is the exception?
o: No; any adult may consent through a power of attorney or a decision-maker
Yes; no exception exists for any person in any circumstance whatever
No; a family member may consent for the person after capacity is lost
Yes; a narrow waiver of final consent where natural death is foreseeable
Q.e: Under federal law at the time of writing, a person must be capable when MAID is provided, except in the narrow situation of a waiver of final consent for people whose natural death is reasonably foreseeable.

Q.q: What is the status of federal advance requests, as described in the chapter?
o: Proposed but not yet law; coming legislation will include advance consent provisions
In force since 2024; the government has announced they will be repealed soon
Law in every province; the government announced no change to the rules
Rejected by Parliament; the government announced no further study of them
Q.e: Federal advance requests have been proposed but are not yet law. In October 2026 the government announced that its coming legislation will include advance consent provisions. Because the area is moving, readers should confirm the current position.

Q.q: What has Quebec done about advance requests?
o: Since 2015, any adult has been able to make one at any time
Since October 30, 2024, people with a serious incurable illness can make one
It has banned them outright for people with Alzheimer’s disease or dementia
It allows them only for people whose sole condition is a mental illness
Q.e: Since October 30, 2024, people diagnosed with a serious and incurable illness that will lead to incapacity, such as early-stage Alzheimer’s disease, can make an advance request to consent in advance to medical aid in dying.

Q.q: Even where a document cannot authorize MAID, how can planning still help?
o: It replaces the need for any assessment by a practitioner or a witness
It allows the decision-maker to consent to MAID on the person’s behalf
It permits the decision-maker to waive final consent on the person’s behalf
It records your views on quality of life, giving decision-makers a clearer picture
Q.e: Your personal care document and conversations can record how you feel about quality of life, dependence, and suffering, which gives your decision-maker and care team a clearer picture of your values.

Q.q: Why should a person who may want MAID in the future speak to a doctor early?
o: Doctors may only assess patients over 80 who are living in hospital
A request must be filed ten years before it can be used
Assessments, the request, and any waiver arrangement take time while capacity remains
Early requests are automatically approved by the province for any adult
Q.e: If you want to be considered for MAID in the future, say so to your doctor early, because the assessments, the written request, and a waiver arrangement can take time to arrange while you still have capacity.

Q.q: How do families react to MAID, and what does an early, repeated conversation usually do?
o: All families agree at once; it usually increases the chance of conflict
Reactions are identical; it usually delays the practitioner’s assessment by weeks
Families rarely react at all; it usually replaces any written request
Reactions differ; it usually reduces the chance of conflict at the bedside
Q.e: Families react differently, some relieved and some finding it hard to accept. An honest conversation, held early and repeated, usually reduces the chance of conflict at the bedside and gives the family time to say what needs to be said.

Q.q: What practical help exists if a practitioner objects to providing MAID?
o: The objecting practitioner must provide it anyway, whatever the personal grounds
The family must find a lawyer to appeal the refusal to a court
The hospital pharmacy appoints a replacement practitioner for the patient
Coordination services help find assessors; the objector helps connect the patient
Q.e: Many provinces have a coordination service that helps patients find assessors and providers, and a practitioner who objects is expected to help connect the patient with someone who will consider the request. In Quebec the facility’s director must find another professional.

Q.q: Which planning decisions does the chapter suggest making in advance?
o: Which bank holds your account, who files your return, and who pays fees
Who will be with you, where you want to be, and what happens afterward
Which court hears your case, who pays the fee, and who keeps records
Which practitioner owns the facility, who writes the will, and who inherits
Q.e: Decide in advance who will be with you, where you want to be, and what you would like to happen afterward. Ask your doctor or regional health authority how the process works where you live.

Q.q: How does MAID connect to donation and to the funeral and estate chapters?
o: It cancels donation; funeral rules differ and estates always need a court
It requires donation; estate duties differ for every death by MAID
It can combine with donation if planned early; later duties are unchanged
It rules out funerals; executor duties are reduced for such a death
Q.e: Some people combine MAID with organ or tissue donation, which must be planned early because it needs coordination. Funeral and burial wishes apply equally to a death by MAID, and executor duties in Chapters 11 and 12 are the same.

Q.q: What support continues after the death, and what is 9-8-8?
o: Legal aid for beneficiaries of the estate; the probate court’s own helpline
Bereavement counselling through hospices and community groups; the national Suicide Crisis Helpline
Tax relief for grieving families; the Public Guardian and Trustee’s helpline
Funeral subsidies for grieving families; the hospital’s patient billing line
Q.e: Hospice societies and community groups provide bereavement counselling for those who have lost someone this way. For anyone struggling with thoughts of ending their life outside the process, 9-8-8 is the national Suicide Crisis Helpline.

Q.q: In Ontario, who holds the first right to decide funeral arrangements, and what must the person show a funeral provider?
o: The eldest child; a signed letter from the family doctor
The estate trustee; photo identification and proof of authority
The spouse; a copy of the will certified by a notary
The nearest relative; a receipt for the funeral deposit
Q.e: In Ontario the order begins with the estate trustee, the executor named in the will or appointed by a court, then the spouse, adult children, and parents. The person making arrangements must show photo identification and proof of authority.

Q.q: In British Columbia, who ranks after the executor, and what happens when people of equal rank disagree?
o: The spouse, then adult children; the eldest decides unless the court is asked
The eldest child, then the spouse; the youngest decides, or the funeral provider chooses
Adult grandchildren, then the spouse; the majority decides, or a notary then rules
The spouse, then siblings; the executor decides, or the coroner then rules in dispute
Q.e: In British Columbia the order is usually the executor, then the spouse, adult children, adult grandchildren, and further relatives. If people of equal rank disagree, the eldest decides, and a person who wants sole control can apply to the Supreme Court.

Q.q: Why is naming an executor also a decision about your funeral, and what weight do written instructions carry in British Columbia?
o: The executor decides first; written wishes bind unless unreasonable, impractical, or a hardship
The executor decides last; written wishes are only suggestions for the family to consider
The executor may choose any provider; written wishes apply only when the contract was prepaid
The executor shares the right equally; written wishes apply only to a cremation service
Q.e: Because the executor holds the first right to decide, naming a trusted executor is also a decision about your funeral. In British Columbia, written instructions in a will or pre-need contract must be followed unless unreasonable, impractical, or cause hardship.

Q.q: Margaret’s son is her executor, but she is closer to her daughter. If she says nothing about her funeral, what is the likely result, and what would help?
o: Her daughter holds legal authority and the two may disagree; a new will naming her
Both children decide jointly by law without dispute; a court application is needed
Her son holds authority and they may disagree; a short written note
The funeral provider decides for the family; a note from the executor is required
Q.e: If nothing is said, Margaret’s son as executor will hold the legal authority, and the two children may disagree about a church service or cremation. A short written note in Margaret’s own words would settle most of that.

Q.q: Why does the chapter warn against putting funeral wishes only in your will?
o: Wills are often read after the funeral; a deposit box may be sealed
Wills cannot mention funerals, so the executor would have to refuse such wishes
Wills become public, and the provider may then raise its prices for the family
Wills take effect only after probate, and a burial may not wait for that
Q.e: Wills are often read after the funeral has taken place, and a safe-deposit box may be sealed or hard to open. Put your wishes in a separate note that your executor and family can see right away, and tell them where it is.

Q.q: Which pairing correctly describes burial and cremation variations?
o: Burial only in a cemetery plot; ashes buried or kept at home, never scattered anywhere
Burial in a plot or mausoleum only; ashes scattered only on private land owned by family
Burial in a natural ground only; ashes placed only in a columbarium niche at a cemetery
Burial in a plot, mausoleum, or green ground; ashes buried, niched, kept, or scattered
Q.e: Burial can be in a cemetery plot, a mausoleum, or a natural or green burial ground. After cremation, ashes may be buried, placed in a columbarium niche, kept, scattered, or a combination.

Q.q: What is alkaline hydrolysis, and how does Ontario treat it?
o: A flame-based process leaving ashes; prohibited by law
A water-based process leaving bone fragments; recognized alongside cremation
A freezing process preserving the body; recognized as burial
A chemical process for embalming; required before cremation
Q.e: Alkaline hydrolysis is a water-based process that reduces the body to bone fragments, and Ontario recognizes it alongside cremation. A burial permit is needed for cremation, burial, or alkaline hydrolysis.

Q.q: Which statement about Ontario’s practical rules is correct?
o: Embalming is always required; the death must be registered only after the burial occurs
Embalming is optional, and a permit is needed only if the family chooses cremation
Embalming is required for cremation, and no registration is needed for the permit
Embalming is not required; the death is registered and a burial permit obtained
Q.e: In Ontario, embalming is not required. The death must be registered with the local municipality, and a burial permit is then needed for cremation, burial, or alkaline hydrolysis.

Q.q: Under the chapter, where may ashes be scattered in Ontario, and what should you do before choosing a special place?
o: Private property with consent, or unoccupied Crown land where no signs prohibit it
Any municipal park without permission, provided the weather is calm and no one objects
Any private property without consent, provided the cemetery rules are checked afterward
Only a registered cemetery, and only after checking with the family doctor first
Q.e: Ashes may be scattered on private property with the landowner’s consent, or on unoccupied Crown land, including water, if no signs prohibit it. Municipal land requires checking local by-laws, so confirm that the place is permitted.

Q.q: If cost is a concern in Ontario, which statement fits the chapter?
o: Items must come from the provider alone; apply to the municipality after signing
Items may come from unlicensed sellers if accepted; apply to the municipality before signing
Providers need not show prices; the municipality pays any shortfall that is left over
Only licensed providers may sell urns; municipal help is automatic for every family
Q.e: In Ontario you can buy caskets and monuments from unlicensed businesses if your provider will accept them, and providers must offer a range of prices. Municipal help must be applied for before signing a contract and usually limits the choices.

Q.q: How do pre-planning and pre-paying differ?
o: Pre-planning records your wishes; pre-paying is paying ahead, and you can do the first alone
Pre-planning means paying in advance; pre-paying records wishes, and each requires the other
Both mean paying in advance; the only difference between them is the provider chosen
Both mean recording wishes; the only difference between them is whether a notary signs
Q.e: Pre-planning means deciding what you want and recording it, while pre-paying means paying in advance. They are separate, and Ontario’s guidance says you can plan without prepaying, with most providers keeping your plans on record at no cost.

Q.q: Which item must an Ontario prepaid contract include?
o: The purchaser only, a price estimate, and a promise to refund in full
The recipient only, the provider’s licence number, and the executor’s name as witness
The provider, a blank price list, and the notary’s seal on every page
The purchaser, recipient, provider, services, cancellation rights, and commissions
Q.e: In Ontario a prepaid contract must name the purchaser, the recipient, and the provider, list the services and supplies, and state the terms, cancellation rights, any commissions the provider receives for recommending products, and applicable taxes.

Q.q: Which pairing describes prepayment methods and Ontario protection?
o: A loan or a lease; a bank guarantees all licensed providers against loss
A trust only; the municipality insures licensed providers against any failure
A trust or insurance; the Prepaid Funeral Services Compensation Fund covers licensed providers
Insurance only; the executor insures licensed providers against loss of funds
Q.e: Prepayment can be made through a trust, in which a bank or trustee holds the money, or through insurance. Ontario’s licensed funeral providers are covered by the Prepaid Funeral Services Compensation Fund, and contracts from July 1, 2012 guarantee the prepaid amount.

Q.q: Which pairing of cancellation rules is described?
o: Ontario: full refund within 15 days, then a fee of 30 percent; BC: 30 days for refund
Ontario: no refund at any time after signing; BC: 10 days for a partial refund
Ontario: full refund at any time; BC: no refund once the contract is signed
Ontario: full refund within 30 days, then 10 percent up to $350; BC: 15 days
Q.e: In Ontario, cancelling within 30 days returns all your money, and afterwards the provider may keep a cancellation fee of 10 percent of the trust amount, up to $350. British Columbia gives 15 days to cancel for any reason with a full refund.

Q.q: Which practice does Quebec’s Consumer Protection Act restrict for prearranged funeral services, and what practical caution does the chapter give?
o: Home visits of any kind; always decide on the first visit
Unrequested solicitation, including by telephone; never feel pressured to decide in one visit
Written contracts; always choose the most expensive package
Price lists; always avoid comparing providers
Q.e: Quebec vendors may not solicit unless you request it, may not solicit by telephone or in a hospital, and must follow limits for home visits. The chapter adds that you should never feel pressured to decide in a single visit and should compare providers.

Q.q: At what age can a person register as an organ and tissue donor in Ontario, and is a signed donor card enough?
o: At least 18; yes, a signed card is sufficient proof of consent
At least 21; no, only a family vote can confirm consent
At least 14; yes, a card signed by a parent is enough
At least 16; no, only the registry record confirms consent
Q.e: In Ontario you can register as an organ and tissue donor if you are at least 16, using your health card, online, in person, or by mail. A signed donor card is not enough, because only the registry record confirms consent.

Q.q: After a death in Ontario, who checks the donor registry, and how do families usually respond to a documented decision?
o: The funeral provider, after which families almost always overturn the decision
The municipal clerk, after which families almost always delay the decision
The Trillium Gift of Life Network; families almost always honour it
The coroner’s office, after which families almost always ignore the decision
Q.e: After a death the Trillium Gift of Life Network checks the registry and reaffirms the decision with the family. Ontario’s guidance says families almost always honour a donation decision when they have evidence of it, and you can update or withdraw your status at any time.

Q.q: How does whole body donation differ from organ and tissue donation?
o: It supports teaching and research through a school of anatomy; a separate program
It helps living recipients, uses the donor registry, and is the very same program
It supports funerals, uses the funeral provider, and is the same program as organ donation
It helps transplant patients, uses the hospital, and is a mandatory program for all donors
Q.e: Organ and tissue donation helps living recipients, while whole body donation supports medical teaching and research. They are different programs with different processes, and one decision does not cover the other.

Q.q: Which reasons may a school of anatomy give for declining a body?
o: A prepaid contract, a will, a funeral plan, or a family dispute over the body
A burial permit, a registry entry, a donor card, or an unpaid administrative fee
An autopsy, embalming, certain infections, or no current need
An executor’s absence, a missing notary, or a registration filed one day late
Q.e: A school may decline a body that has been autopsied or embalmed, has had an amputation, or has certain infectious diseases, or if it does not currently need donations. Donations normally go to the school nearest the donor’s home.

Q.ti: Telling the right people about donation
Q.q: Why does the chapter urge telling family and doctors about a donation decision, and what must be coordinated if MAID is also planned?
o: Donation is delayed for months; combining it with MAID is prohibited outright
Donation usually needs prompt action; combining it with MAID needs coordination
Donation is automatic; combining it with MAID needs no coordination at all
Donation is decided by the executor; combining it with MAID is mandatory by law
Q.e: Because donation usually requires prompt action at or near death, tell your family and doctors. If you are considering medical assistance in dying, talk to your team early, because combining that process with donation requires careful coordination.

Q.q: What should a short funeral plan cover?
o: The cost of the estate, the executor’s fee, the tax rate, and the probate date
Only the preferred provider and the price, with all other details left to the family
Burial or cremation, service type, resting place, preferred provider, prepaid contract, cultural practices
Only the prepaid contract, with all wishes left to the executor to decide later
Q.e: A short, clear document should say whether you prefer burial or cremation, the kind of service, where you would like to be buried or your ashes placed, your preferred provider, any prepaid contract, and religious or cultural practices. A page or two is plenty.

Q.q: Whom should you tell about your funeral plan, and where should the original be recorded?
o: The funeral provider only; recorded in the will’s residue clause and nowhere else
The beneficiaries only; recorded in a sealed envelope left at the bank
The executor, spouse, children, and a close friend; recorded in Appendix B
A notary only; recorded in the municipality’s records after the funeral
Q.e: Tell the person who will have authority, usually your executor, and also your spouse, children, and a close friend, and give them copies. Store the original with your other planning documents and record its location on the document organizer in Appendix B.

Q.q: Which practical details can you add to your funeral note?
o: Which assets the estate holds, who owes the estate, and which tax return applies
Which court hears disputes, which lawyer drafts the will, and which executor serves
Which bank pays the bills, which insurer renews, and which landlord is told
Who writes the notice, which photo, who speaks, and the service location
Q.e: Many families struggle with practical details such as who will write the notice, which photograph to use, who will speak, and where the service will be held. Specific instructions reduce stress and let family members focus on grieving.

Q.q: Who normally pays for the funeral, and what can spare the family the burden?
o: The family, with no repayment from the estate; a larger life insurance policy for them
The estate, though a relative often pays first and is repaid; a prepaid contract helps
The provider, with repayment after probate; a longer cancellation period for deposits
The municipality, with no repayment from the estate; a larger will with more gifts
Q.e: Funeral costs are normally paid from the estate, but the provider may want payment first, so a family member often pays and is repaid. A prepaid contract or small dedicated account spares the family that burden.

Q.q: Which statement about the order of tasks for a prepaid contract is consistent with the chapter?
o: Keep it with related insurance and give the executor a copy
Keep it private and give no copy to anyone, including the executor
Give it only to the funeral provider and the bank holding the trust
Store it in the will so it is only read after the funeral
Q.e: Keep prepaid contracts together with any related insurance policy and give a copy of any contract to your executor. A prepaid contract that nobody knows about is a common source of wasted money, because the family may buy a second funeral.

Q.q: In Ontario, what should the family do after an expected death at home under palliative care, and what document records the cause of death?
o: Call the coroner first, and then complete the Statement of Death yourselves
The doctor caring for the person; the Medical Certificate of Death
Contact the municipal clerk first, who then issues the burial permit directly
Call the funeral provider first, who then signs the cremation certificate
Q.e: For an expected death in Ontario, such as at home under palliative care, the family contacts the doctor who was caring for the person. The attending doctor or a coroner then completes the Medical Certificate of Death, which states the cause of death.

Q.q: What should a family do for an unexpected death, or if no doctor is available or the circumstances are unclear?
o: Call the funeral provider first; contact the municipal clerk if the cause is unclear
Wait for the executor to arrive; contact the bank if the cause is unclear
Call the family doctor’s office only; contact the notary if the cause is unclear
Call emergency services; contact the coroner’s office if unclear
Q.e: For an unexpected death they call emergency services. If no doctor or emergency service is available, or the circumstances are unclear, they contact the local coroner’s office. A medical professional must certify the death before it can be registered.

Q.q: After confirming the death, whom does the chapter say to contact next?
o: The funeral provider, close family, the executor, and the employer or care facility
The Canada Revenue Agency, the bank, the passport office, and the credit agencies
The land registry, the insurer, the credit agencies, and the court registry staff
The municipal clerk, the court, the pension plan, and the family’s own lawyer
Q.e: The second step is to contact the funeral provider, if one is being used, and tell the people who need to know now: close family, the executor, and the employer or care facility. The funeral provider will usually guide the next steps.

Q.q: Which approach to early decisions does the chapter recommend?
o: Sell the house quickly, cancel the accounts, and publish the funeral date widely
Distribute the belongings at once and leave the home unattended during the funeral
Cancel all the accounts first and announce the funeral date on every public notice
Avoid large decisions; secure the home, arrange pet care, be cautious sharing the funeral date
Q.e: There is no need to sell a house, cancel accounts, or distribute belongings in the first days. Do secure the home, arrange care for pets and dependants, and be cautious about sharing the date and place of the funeral, since thieves sometimes target empty homes.

Q.q: How did Margaret’s written note help her family in the example?
o: It named her beneficiaries, so that her family could skip probate altogether
It told them whom to call and where papers were, so they could grieve
It cancelled her accounts, so that her family could skip the notifications
It appointed her attorney, so that her family could skip the registration
Q.e: Because Margaret had written down who to call and where her papers were, the family spent the first day grieving rather than searching.

Q.q: In Ontario, who usually oversees registration of a death, and what do the director and informant complete?
o: A funeral director; the Statement of Death, filed with the municipal clerk
A family member; the Medical Certificate, submitted to the coroner’s office
A notary; the death certificate, submitted to the court registry for approval
A lawyer; the burial permit, submitted to the bank holding the estate
Q.e: In Ontario, a funeral director usually oversees registration. The director and an informant, normally a family member, complete the Statement of Death, and the documents are submitted to the municipal clerk’s office, usually where the death occurred.

Q.q: Which sequence is correct for Ontario?
o: The burial permit first; then registration, and last the death certificate
The death certificate first; then registration, and last the burial permit
Registration first; then the burial permit and the death certificate
Registration last, after the burial permit and the death certificate are both issued
Q.e: Registration must happen before a burial permit can be issued, and the permit is required for burial, cremation, or alkaline hydrolysis. Registration is also needed before a death certificate can be issued.

Q.q: Who can apply for a certified copy of an Ontario death registration, and why order several?
o: Any friend of the family; one copy is accepted everywhere without question
Only next of kin or the executor; many institutions may each want a copy
Only the funeral provider; each institution accepts a simple photocopy instead
Only a lawyer; one certified copy is the most the law allows to be issued
Q.e: In Ontario only the next of kin or the executor can apply for a certified copy, and there is no limit on how many. Banks, insurers, pension plans, government offices, and land registries may each ask for an original or certified copy.

Q.q: Why check a death certificate as soon as it arrives?
o: Errors can never be corrected later, so every copy must be reissued in full
Errors affect only the funeral provider, so the executor need not check them
Errors in names or dates are easier to correct early than months later
Errors are automatically fixed by the municipal clerk without any request
Q.e: Check the certificate for errors in name, date of birth, marital status, and parents’ names. Corrections are easier early than months later, when the executor is trying to transfer property.

Q.q: In Quebec, where are deaths recorded, and what should Quebec Pension Plan recipients’ families do?
o: In the civil status register; contact Retraite Québec
In the Superior Court registry; contact Service Canada only
In the municipal clerk’s office; contact the CRA only
In the notarial register; contact the Public Guardian only
Q.e: In Quebec deaths are recorded in the civil status register, and the funeral director or a family member provides the information. Quebec residents who received Quebec Pension Plan benefits should also contact Retraite Québec.

Q.q: Which three offices does federal guidance list as time-sensitive, and why does speed matter?
o: The passport office, Equifax, and Canada Post; delays can cause late fees on the estate
The land registry, the court, and the coroner; delays can cause the loss of property
The bank, the insurer, and the employer; delays can cause the loss of final wages
The CRA, CPP and OAS, and the Canada Disability Benefit; delays cause overpayments
Q.e: Federal guidance lists the Canada Revenue Agency, the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security, and the Canada Disability Benefit as time-sensitive. Delays can lead to benefit overpayments that the estate must repay.

Q.q: For CPP and OAS payments, which statement is correct?
o: Report to Service Canada with the SIN; the estate keeps the month-of-death payment
Report to the bank only; the estate must repay the month-of-death payment in full
Report to the CRA only; the estate keeps all of the payments issued afterward
Report to the funeral provider; the estate keeps nothing from any payment at all
Q.e: Report the death to Service Canada with the deceased’s SIN ready. The estate is entitled to the payment for the month of death, while payments issued after that month must be returned, even if already cashed.

Q.q: What does the chapter say about the Social Insurance Number and a passport?
o: The executor notifies the SIN program; destroy the passport without any notice
Territories notify the SIN program; keep the passport for the estate to use
Provinces notify the SIN program; mail the passport with a certificate copy and letter
The bank notifies the SIN program; return the passport to the family unopened
Q.e: In provinces the vital statistics agency notifies the SIN program, while in the territories or outside Canada you must send the number and proof of death to Service Canada. A valid passport should be mailed to the Passport Program with a death certificate copy.

Q.q: Which other steps does the chapter mention to reduce risk and cancel services?
o: Notify the court, cancel the will, and withdraw the probate application at once
Notify the employer, cancel the funeral, and withdraw the donor registration at once
Notify the coroner, cancel the pension, and withdraw the burial permit at once
Notify Equifax and TransUnion, forward the mail, and withdraw pending immigration applications
Q.e: Notify the credit reporting agencies, Equifax and TransUnion, to reduce fraud risk, arrange mail forwarding with Canada Post, and withdraw pending immigration, permanent resident, or citizenship applications through Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada.

Q.q: In Ontario, what applies to an accessible parking permit and a driver’s licence?
o: Return the permit within 30 months; a licence refund is always available to the estate
Keep the permit for the estate to use; a licence refund is never available at all
Return the permit within 30 days; a licence refund may apply with six months left
Return the permit within one week; a licence refund is paid to the executor directly
Q.e: In Ontario an accessible parking permit must be returned to ServiceOntario within 30 days. A driver’s licence can be cancelled at a ServiceOntario centre, and a refund may be available if six or more months remain and there are no outstanding fines.

Q.q: Which three Canada Pension Plan benefits are most common, and how are they obtained?
o: The death benefit, survivor’s pension, and children’s benefit; each requires an application
The retirement pension, disability pension, and child tax benefit; each is automatic
The death benefit, the OAS pension, and the guaranteed supplement; each is automatic
The survivor’s pension, the dental plan, and the child tax benefit; each is automatic
Q.e: Three Canada Pension Plan benefits are the most common: the death benefit, the survivor’s pension, and the children’s benefit. All require an application, and none is paid automatically.

Q.q: For deaths on or after January 1, 2025, what is the maximum CPP death benefit, and when should the executor apply?
o: $2,500 with no top-up possible; apply within six months of the death
$5,000 with a possible top-up; apply within 60 days of the death
$10,000 with a possible $5,000 top-up; apply within 30 days of the death
$5,000 with no basic amount; apply within one year of the death
Q.e: The CPP death benefit is a one-time $2,500 plus a possible $2,500 top-up, for a maximum of $5,000, for deaths on or after January 1, 2025. Federal guidance advises applying within 60 days; processing takes six to twelve weeks.

Q.q: Who qualifies for the CPP survivor’s pension, and what is the pension for a survivor aged 65 or older who receives no other CPP benefit?
o: Only the legal spouse; 37.5 percent of the contributor’s retirement pension
Any dependent child of the contributor; 100 percent of the retirement pension
Only a partner of five years or more; 50 percent of the retirement pension
A spouse or partner of one year or more; 60 percent of the pension
Q.e: A common-law partner is someone who lived with the contributor in a conjugal relationship for at least one year. For a survivor aged 65 or older with no other CPP benefit, the pension is 60 percent of the contributor’s retirement pension.

Q.q: Which statements about the survivor’s pension are correct?
o: Back payments cover five years; remarriage ends it; children under 18 may qualify for benefits
Back payments are unlimited; remarriage ends it; children never qualify for any benefits
Back payments cover twelve months only; remarriage does not end it; children under 25 may qualify
Back payments cover one month; remarriage reduces it; children under 21 may qualify for benefits
Q.e: Back payments cover only up to twelve months, so apply early. Remarriage does not end the pension, and children under 25 may qualify for children’s benefits.

Q.q: In Quebec, which agency runs the QPP, and what does a surviving spouse generally receive from a workplace pension for a death in retirement?
o: Service Canada; a joint and survivor pension of at least 100 percent in every case
The Curateur public; a lump sum equal to one full year of the member’s pension
Revenu Québec; a joint and survivor pension of at least 20 percent of the pension
Retraite Québec; a joint pension of at least 60 percent unless the spouse agreed less
Q.e: The Quebec Pension Plan is run by Retraite Québec, with its own death, survivor’s, and orphan’s benefits. For a death in retirement, a surviving spouse is generally entitled to a joint and survivor pension of at least 60 percent, unless the spouse agreed to less.

Q.q: How does the chapter suggest organizing the first weeks?
o: A binder with a page per organization, reference numbers, and one master record keeper
A single phone call to the bank, with no written record kept of what was said
A shared email account, with each person keeping a separate private record
A spreadsheet kept only by the funeral provider and shared with no one else
Q.e: A simple notebook or binder, with one page per organization, lets you record who you spoke to, what they asked for, and what was promised. Keep a list of reference numbers, scan every letter, and designate one person to keep the master record.

Q.q: Does most early work require probate, and what should an executor do if an institution asks for a grant?
o: Yes, every task needs probate; keep a list of the items already finished
No, most need a death certificate and ID; list items waiting for a grant
No, no task ever needs probate; keep a list of the items that were refused
Yes, banks never ask for probate; keep a list of the items completed so far
Q.e: Most early tasks need only a death certificate and the executor’s identification. Some institutions deal only with a person holding a grant of probate, so keep a list of the things waiting for one.

Q.q: How should a family respond to a demand for payment from the estate after an obituary appears?
o: Pay quickly by gift card to avoid penalties that the caller says will be added
Check it independently; real creditors write claims, and unusual contacts go to the executor
Wire the funds at once if the caller knows the name of the person who died
Ignore every creditor permanently, including legitimate ones who write to the estate
Q.e: Scammers read obituaries and may pose as creditors or officials. Government agencies do not demand immediate payment by gift card or wire, and a legitimate creditor will put a claim in writing. Check any request independently before paying.

Q.q: What does the chapter say about looking after yourself while handling an estate?
o: Handle every task alone, skip breaks, and politely refuse every offer of help
Delegate every task to the bank, skip family contact, and wait for a letter to arrive
Share the work, take breaks, accept help, and ask providers or doctors for support
Postpone every task for a year, avoid advisers, and hire only a notary to act
Q.e: Executors and family members who are grieving are also asked to handle forms, phone calls, and decisions. Share the work, take breaks, and accept offers of help, and the funeral provider, a hospice bereavement program, your family doctor, or a lawyer can point you to support.

Q.q: The chapter’s planning prompt asks whether an executor could find your SIN, accounts, policies, and pension details. What does it recommend?
o: Keep every detail in your own memory only, and tell no one at all about it
Prepare one page now that saves the executor the most time
Share your details with your bank only, and give nobody else any copies
Wait until a lawyer asks for the details before writing anything down at all
Q.e: The chapter asks readers whether their executor could find their Social Insurance Number, list of accounts, insurance policies, and pension details, and what one page they could prepare now that would save the executor the most time.

Q.q: What does probate confirm, and what is the Ontario document called?
o: That the estate owes no tax and is ready to close; a Certificate of Clearance for Estate Trustees
That the deceased had capacity when the will was made; a Notice of Estate Administration
That a will is valid and the executor has authority; a Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee
That all beneficiaries agree to the will’s terms; a Grant of Authority for Distribution
Q.e: Probate is the court process that confirms the will is valid and the named executor has legal authority to act. In Ontario the resulting document is a Certificate of Appointment of Estate Trustee, and British Columbia calls it a grant of probate.

Q.q: Which two kinds of assets generally pass outside the estate without probate?
o: Real estate in the sole name and investment accounts above a bank’s threshold
Jointly owned property with survivorship and accounts with a named beneficiary
Vehicles and household contents and accounts held in trust for a creditor
Property left in the residue and property given to a charity by the will
Q.e: Jointly owned property with a right of survivorship, and accounts or policies with a named beneficiary, generally pass outside the estate and do not need probate. Sole-name real estate and large accounts often cannot be transferred without a grant.

Q.q: Margaret Osei’s house in Hamilton is in her sole name, and her daughter holds a joint account with her. What follows?
o: Her son needs no certificate for the house; the joint account must go through the estate
Her daughter needs the certificate for the house; the joint account passes to the son
Her son needs a certificate only for the joint account; the house passes by survivorship
Her son will likely need a certificate for the house; the joint account may pass outside the estate
Q.e: A house in Margaret’s sole name will almost certainly need a certificate before her son can sell it. A joint account with her daughter may pass outside the estate, so only a review of each asset shows what needs probate.

Q.q: How does Quebec differ in the way a will gains authority?
o: Every will needs a court grant; notarial wills need two witnesses
A holograph will needs no verification; notarial wills need a court order
A notarial will needs no court approval; other wills need verification
Every will is verified by the land registry; a liquidator then files it
Q.e: In Quebec a will made before a notary does not need court approval, but a holograph will or a will made before witnesses must be verified by the court or a notary. This is why many Quebecers choose notarial wills.

Q.q: How should an executor decide whether to apply for probate, and who sets the thresholds at which banks insist on it?
o: Weigh cost against delay; each institution sets its own threshold, so ask each one
Always apply at once; the court sets one threshold for every institution in the province
Never apply for small estates; the province sets a threshold of $50,000 for all banks
Apply only if a beneficiary objects; the Law Society sets the threshold for institutions
Q.e: The decision is practical: the executor weighs fees and legal help against the delay of dealing with institutions that insist on a grant. Institutions set their own thresholds, so ask each of them rather than assuming.

Q.q: Under Ontario’s Estate Administration Tax, what would an estate valued at $240,000 pay, and what is the rule?
o: $3,600; nothing up to $50,000, then $15 per $1,000 on the whole value
$2,850; nothing up to $50,000, then $15 per $1,000 above that
$2,850; nothing up to $25,000, then $6 per $1,000 above that
$3,600; nothing up to $25,000, then $14 per $1,000 above that
Q.e: Estates of $50,000 or less pay no tax. Above that, the tax is $15 per $1,000, with the value rounded up to the nearest $1,000, so an estate of $240,000 pays $2,850.

Q.q: Which items are included in, and which are excluded from, the value for Ontario’s tax?
o: Included: Ontario real estate less mortgages; excluded: assets with named beneficiaries
Included: funeral costs and debts as deductions; excluded: bank and investment accounts
Included: jointly owned assets that pass automatically; excluded: vehicles and other property
Included: real estate outside Ontario; excluded: Ontario real estate with a mortgage on it
Q.e: The value includes Ontario real estate less mortgages and liens, bank and investment accounts, vehicles, and other property. It excludes real estate outside Ontario, assets with named beneficiaries, and jointly owned assets that pass automatically. Funeral costs and debts cannot be deducted.

Q.q: Who pays probate fees, and how reliable are the published provincial figures?
o: The executor pays them personally; fee schedules never change, so rely on the figures
The beneficiaries pay them equally; fees are identical across provinces, so no check is needed
The lawyer pays them first; fee schedules change yearly, so ask the lawyer only
The estate pays them; fee schedules change, so confirm on the court’s website
Q.e: Probate fees are paid by the estate, not by the executor’s own money. Because fee schedules change, treat the published figures as illustrations and confirm the current rate on the court’s website.

Q.q: In Ontario, what must be filed within 180 days after the certificate is issued, and what risks follow false information?
o: An Estate Information Return; a fine of at least $1,000, possible prison, and four years of records
A T3 trust return; a penalty of $25 per day, with a cap of $2,500 in all cases
A clearance certificate request; loss of the executor’s fee and a formal court removal
A notice to creditors; a reassessment of the deceased’s final return without any fine
Q.e: An Estate Information Return is due to the Ministry of Finance within 180 days after the certificate, even if the value is zero. Failing to file or filing false information can mean a fine of at least $1,000, up to two years in prison, or both.

Q.q: Why does the chapter warn against understating the estate’s value?
o: Understated values are simply corrected later by the court, with no penalty for the executor
Understated values reduce the fee, and the chapter treats this as a lawful planning step
Misstated values can bring penalties, a reassessment, and personal liability for the executor
Understated values affect only the beneficiaries, who then receive a smaller share of the estate
Q.e: Underestimating the estate to reduce the fee is a common mistake. Misstated values on an application or information return can lead to penalties, a reassessment, and personal liability for the executor, so report accurately and get help with valuations.

Q.q: What does it mean to say an executor is a fiduciary, and what follows for mistakes made in good faith?
o: The executor must act only for the largest beneficiary; honest mistakes are always forgiven by the court
The executor holds an honorary role; careless decisions are the lawyer’s responsibility alone
The executor must act with loyalty and care for others; good-faith mistakes without proper care may bring personal liability
The executor must act for creditors alone; mistakes in good faith are always paid by the estate
Q.e: A fiduciary must act with loyalty and care for the beneficiaries and creditors. The role is not honorary, and executors may be personally liable even for decisions made in good faith but without proper care.

Q.q: Which pair of duties reflects the basic duties of a common-law executor?
o: Pool estate money with personal funds; keep records only for large payments
Distribute gifts first; locate assets after beneficiaries have been paid in full
Open an account in the beneficiaries’ names; keep records until the funeral ends
Open a separate estate account; keep detailed records, receipts, and invoices
Q.e: The executor must secure the property, list assets and debts, open a separate estate account kept apart from personal money, and keep detailed records, receipts, and invoices. Advice from lawyers and accountants is allowed, and the cost is generally paid from the estate.

Q.q: Which conduct is most likely to draw a claim against an executor?
o: Favouring one beneficiary and reimbursing undocumented expenses
Sending a regular update even when nothing has changed
Paying a lawyer from the estate for advice on liability
Following the will when family members would prefer otherwise
Q.e: Favouring one beneficiary, using estate property personally, mixing estate and personal money, and reimbursing undocumented expenses all draw claims. A neutral, regular update to beneficiaries, even when nothing has changed, reduces suspicion.

Q.q: In Quebec, which sequence reflects the liquidator’s work, and what risk comes from distributing early?
o: Final account, inventory, returns and certificates, closure notice; personal liability for unpaid fees
Returns and certificates, distribution, inventory, closure notice; liability falls on the heirs only
Inventory, closure notice, returns and certificates, final account; personal liability for unpaid taxes
Closure notice, distribution, inventory, final account; liability falls on the notary who verified the will
Q.e: The liquidator prepares a signed inventory, publishes a closure notice, files returns, obtains the federal and Quebec certificates, pays debts, and gives a final account. Distributing before the certificates may mean personal liability for unpaid taxes.

Q.q: Why should an executor ask an adviser about the form of an estate account, and who normally bears the adviser’s cost?
o: To avoid keeping records at all; the executor generally pays the cost
To pool money with the executor’s own; the beneficiaries generally pay the cost
To skip creditors’ claims entirely; the lawyer generally absorbs the cost
To keep estate money separate and correct; the estate generally pays the cost
Q.e: The chapter’s lawyer prompt asks what should be in the estate account, and the executor must keep estate money out of personal accounts. Advice from lawyers and accountants is allowed and often wise, with the cost generally paid from the estate.

Q.q: In what order are payments generally made before beneficiaries receive gifts?
o: Credit cards, then the funeral, then gifts, then taxes and administration costs
Funeral and administration costs, then debts including taxes, loans, and credit cards
Cash gifts, then the funeral costs, then taxes, then any remaining debts of the deceased
Taxes, then the residue, then funeral costs, then the cost of administering the estate
Q.e: The funeral and the costs of administering the estate are generally priority expenses. The executor then pays the deceased’s debts, including taxes, loans, and credit cards, before distributing. Rules on order differ by province, so a doubtful estate calls for a lawyer first.

Q.q: What is the most dangerous mistake in distribution, and what protects the executor against unpaid income tax?
o: Distributing too late; the Estate Information Return
Paying the funeral first; the notice to creditors
Holding back a reserve; the probate certificate
Distributing too early; the federal clearance certificate
Q.e: If the executor pays out the estate and a debt or tax bill then appears, the executor may have to cover it personally. For income tax the main protection is the federal clearance certificate, and holding back a reserve is standard practice.

Q.q: Which describes the order of gifts in distribution and how an executor usually closes the account?
o: Specific items, then cash gifts, then the residue; an account with a signed release
The residue, then cash gifts, then specific items; an account with no release
Cash gifts, then the residue, then specific items; a verbal approval by the heirs
Specific items, then the residue, then cash gifts; a notice in the local newspaper
Q.e: Gifts of specific items go to the named people, cash gifts are paid, and the residue is divided among the residuary beneficiaries. The executor usually prepares an account of all money in and out and asks beneficiaries to approve it and sign a release.

Q.q: A beneficiary is not satisfied with the executor’s account. What may the beneficiary do, and what is that called in some provinces?
o: Ask the CRA to audit the estate; clearing the accounts
Ask the court to review the accounts; passing the accounts
Ask the notary to reverse the gifts; verifying the accounts
Ask the bank to freeze the estate; closing the accounts
Q.e: A beneficiary who is not satisfied may ask the court to review the accounts, which is called passing the accounts in some provinces. Asking for approval and a signed release is the usual way an executor reduces that risk.

Q.q: When a beneficiary has died first or an asset has been sold, what should an executor do and what planning helps?
o: Make a fair-sounding decision alone; naming a single residuary heir
Divide the gift equally among the others; naming joint owners
Wait for the beneficiaries to agree; naming a professional executor
Seek advice before acting; naming backup beneficiaries
Q.e: A beneficiary may have died first, a named asset may have been sold, or the estate may be too small to pay every gift. The executor should seek advice rather than decide alone, and planning such as naming backup beneficiaries from Chapter 3 helps.

Q.q: On what does an executor’s compensation depend, and what should an executor keep from the start?
o: The size of the probate fee alone; a copy of the funeral invoice only
The quality of the work and supporting accounts; a log of time and tasks
The wishes of the eldest beneficiary; a record of the final return only
The court’s fixed schedule in every province; a list of creditors only
Q.e: Compensation depends on the quality of the work and on the accounts that support it. The court looks at the size and complexity of the estate, the time and skill required, and the care shown, so keep a log of time and tasks from the start.

Q.q: Which professionals are suited to which tasks in a split of roles?
o: A lawyer for probate and liability advice; an accountant for the final return and clearance
An accountant for probate and liability advice; a lawyer for the final return and clearance
A trust company for the final return only; a lawyer for the estate account only
A lawyer for the final return and clearance; a notary for the beneficiary designations only
Q.e: A lawyer can handle probate and give advice on liability, while an accountant can file the final return and manage the clearance certificate. A trust company can act as executor or co-executor for a fee, and many families split the roles.

Q.q: May a person named as executor refuse the role, and who can end the appointment later?
o: Yes, at any time without a court process; only the beneficiaries may remove one later
No, the role cannot be refused once named; only the lawyer may replace an executor
Yes, if they have not begun acting; the court may replace or remove an executor
No, unless the will permits it; the CRA may remove an executor who delays filing
Q.e: A named executor may refuse if they have not begun acting; afterward, giving up needs a formal process. The court can replace an executor who cannot continue, and beneficiaries can ask it to remove one who is not doing the job.

Q.q: Why do many estates take about a year, and what should an executor avoid?
o: Waiting for the funeral, naming the heirs, and renewing the will cause delay; avoid keeping records
Waiting for tax clearance, selling property, and disputes cause delay; avoid pressure to distribute early
Waiting for the probate fee, closing the accounts, and a notary’s fee cause delay; avoid informing heirs
Waiting for the heirs’ birthdays, selling cars, and trust fees cause delay; avoid obtaining valuations
Q.e: Many estates take about a year or longer. Delays often come from waiting for tax clearance, selling property, locating assets, or resolving disputes, so plan for patience, keep beneficiaries informed, and avoid the pressure to distribute early.

Q.q: Which is correct about the planning worksheet’s checklist and the executor’s habits?
o: Keep estate money in a joint account and distribute once the funeral is paid
Keep payment records only for large items and distribute when heirs request it
Keep estate money separate and do not distribute until debts and taxes are clear
Keep estate money with the executor’s own and update heirs only at the close
Q.e: The worksheet checklist reminds the executor to keep estate money separate from personal money, record every payment and receipt, not distribute until debts and taxes are clear, and update the beneficiaries regularly.

Q.q: Does Canada have an inheritance tax, and who bears the tax arising at death?
o: No; the tax falls on the deceased’s final return, paid from the estate
No; the tax falls on each beneficiary, paid from the inheritance
Yes; the tax falls on each beneficiary, paid within 90 days
Yes; the tax falls on the executor, paid from personal funds
Q.e: Canada has no inheritance or estate tax in the sense used elsewhere. Beneficiaries do not normally pay tax on what they receive. The tax arises on the person who died, and the executor pays it from the estate before beneficiaries are paid.

Q.q: Which period does the final return cover, and what becomes of income arising after death?
o: The year before death; the estate becomes the executor’s income
January 1 to the date of death; the estate becomes a separate taxpayer
January 1 to December 31; the estate becomes the spouse’s income
The last twelve months; the estate becomes part of the final return
Q.e: The final return covers the period from January 1 to the date of death. The estate then becomes a separate taxpayer for income that arises after death, and it may need its own return.

Q.q: Why does the chapter advise a conversation with Margaret’s accountant now?
o: Her son must deal with her final return, registered savings, and the question of her principal residence
Her son must pay inheritance tax, her pension, and the question of her will’s validity
Her daughter must file the T3, her bank accounts, and the question of her power of attorney
Her daughter must claim the estate tax credit, her pension, and the question of probate fees
Q.e: When Margaret dies, her son will have to deal with her final return, the tax on her registered savings, and whether the Hamilton home qualifies as her principal residence. A conversation with her accountant now would show him where the paperwork is.

Q.q: In Quebec, with whom do residents file in parallel, and who should help the liquidator?
o: Retraite Québec; a trust company that knows both pension plans
The Public Curator; a lawyer who knows only provincial law
Revenu Québec; a notary or accountant who knows both systems
The Quebec court; a funeral director who knows both systems
Q.e: Quebec residents file in parallel with Revenu Québec, which has its own forms, including a notice that must be filed before distribution. The liquidator should work with a notary or accountant who knows both the federal and Quebec systems.

Q.q: Why is tax an area where executors often need professional help?
o: Tax is simple, and professionals are needed only to sign the forms
Tax is paid by beneficiaries, and professionals are needed to collect it
Tax rules never change, and professionals are needed for the T3 only
Mistakes are expensive, and some reductions need elections made on time
Q.e: Some rules reduce or defer tax, particularly for property passing to a spouse or partner, but they need action and sometimes elections made on time. Mistakes are costly, so an estate lawyer and accountant often save more than their fees.

Q.q: What is the filing deadline for a final return if the person died on March 10, and if the person died on November 20?
o: April 30 of the following year; six months after the date of death
April 30 of the same year; April 30 of the following year
June 15 of the following year; December 31 of the following year
Six months after death; April 30 of the following year
Q.e: A death between January 1 and October 31 gives a due date of April 30 of the following year. A death between November 1 and December 31 gives six months after the date of death.

Q.q: When a business was run and the death occurs up to December 15, what changes and what does not?
o: The payment date becomes June 15 of the next year; the filing deadline does not move
Both dates move to December 31 of the next year; nothing else changes
Neither date changes; instalments become due immediately after death
The filing date becomes June 15 of the next year; the payment deadline does not move
Q.e: If the person or their spouse or partner ran a business, a later filing date of June 15 of the following year applies for deaths up to December 15, but the payment deadline does not move. Instalments are not due after death.

Q.q: Which statement correctly describes a return for rights or things?
o: It covers amounts the estate earns after death; it is required in every case
It covers amounts earned but not yet received at death; it is optional and may reduce tax
It covers the family home’s gain; it is optional and must be filed with the T3
It covers registered plan income; it is required and due on April 30
Q.e: A return for rights or things covers amounts earned but not yet received at death. It is optional, may reduce tax, and is due the later of one year after death or 90 days after the final return’s assessment notice.

Q.q: What penalties apply to a late return with a balance owing, and what happens to unpaid balances?
o: 10 percent plus 2 percent per month, up to 24 months; simple interest starting after one year has passed
5 percent flat with no monthly addition; interest starting only after the notice of assessment is issued
5 percent plus 1 percent per full month to 12 months; compound daily interest after the due date
$25 per day, with a $2,500 maximum; interest starting only after a CRA audit of the late return
Q.e: A late return with a balance owing carries a penalty of 5 percent of the balance plus 1 percent for each full month late, up to 12 months. Unpaid balances accrue compound daily interest from the day after the due date.

Q.ti: The final return is not routine
Q.q: Why does the chapter call treating the final return as routine a common mistake, and what should be on the calendar?
o: Usually the smallest return of all; only the date of the funeral service
Often the largest, most complex return; filing and payment dates
A routine annual return; only the date of the clearance request itself
Always filed by the CRA for the family; only the instalment payment dates
Q.e: The final return is usually the person’s largest and most complex, with registered plan income, property gains, and amounts earned but unpaid. Get professional help and calendar filing and payment dates from the first week.

Q.q: What is a deemed disposition, and what portion of a capital gain is currently included in income?
o: Treatment as having given property to heirs at cost on death; two-thirds
Treatment as having sold capital property at fair market value on death; one-half
Treatment as having sold only the home at market value; one-half
Treatment as having sold registered plans at cost; three-quarters
Q.e: At death a person is treated as having sold all capital property at fair market value, so gains are taxed on the final return though nothing was sold. One-half of a capital gain is included in income; a proposal to raise that was cancelled in 2025.

Q.q: How are registered plans treated, and when can tax be deferred?
o: The full value is added to income at death; a spouse or partner rollover defers tax
Only the growth is added to income at death; a rollover applies to any adult beneficiary
They are exempt on death entirely; a rollover applies only to the estate itself
Their value is split across several years; a rollover applies only to charities named
Q.e: An RRSP or RRIF’s full value is normally added to income in the year of death. A rollover to a surviving spouse or partner’s plan can defer the tax, and similar rules may apply to a dependent child or grandchild.

Q.q: Which problem arises with the principal residence exemption?
o: Only a rented home can be designated each year, which matters with a house and cottage
Only one home can be designated for a given year, which matters with a house and cottage
Two homes can be designated for a year, which matters only for a spouse
No home can be designated by an executor, which matters only for a cottage
Q.e: A gain on a principal residence is generally exempt, claimed by reporting the designation on the final return. With a house and a cottage, only one can be designated for a given year.

Q.q: Why obtain date-of-death valuations for every capital asset?
o: Fair market value that day sets the probate fee and the executor’s compensation
Fair market value that day sets the TX19 fee and the clearance interest rate
Fair market value that day sets the T3 year-end and the estate’s trust number
Fair market value that day sets the gain on the final return and the beneficiary’s cost
Q.e: The executor should obtain valuations as of the date of death for every capital asset, because the fair market value on that day sets both the gain on the final return and the cost for the beneficiary who receives the asset.

Q.q: Property bypasses probate by joint ownership or designation. How does that affect tax?
o: Tax is never due on those assets, and the executor has no role in recovery
Tax is due only from the recipients, and the final return excludes the assets
Tax may still arise on the final return, and the executor may recover it from recipients
Tax is due only if probate is applied for, and the executor pays it personally
Q.e: Assets that pass outside the estate by joint ownership or designation still generate tax on the deceased’s final return where the deemed disposition applies, even though they bypass probate. The executor may have to recover the tax from the people who received them.

Q.q: When must an estate file a T3, and who may report a CPP death benefit alone?
o: Only when it holds real estate in the province; the executor, in every single case
Only when probate is granted by the court; the estate, if the benefit exceeds $5,000
When any beneficiary asks for one in writing; the CRA, if the benefit is paid late
When it earns income or distributes property; a beneficiary, if the benefit is the only income
Q.e: An estate may need a T3 if it earns income, such as interest or dividends, or distributes property. If a CPP or QPP death benefit is its only income, the beneficiary can report it personally.

Q.q: What advantage does a graduated rate estate have, and how long does it last?
o: Taxed at the top rate on every dollar; up to 12 months from death
Taxed at normal graduated rates; up to 36 months from death
Taxed at half the normal rate; up to 60 months from death
Taxed only on capital gains; up to 90 days from death
Q.e: For up to 36 months, a qualifying estate is taxed at normal graduated rates rather than the top rate on every dollar. After 36 months it loses that status and its income is taxed at the highest rate.

Q.q: How is the designation made, and what may the executor choose?
o: By filing the TX19 form separately; a year-end within 36 months of death
By writing a letter to the CRA; a year-end of December 31 each year
By ticking the box on the first T3; a year-end within 12 months
By asking the court for an order; a year-end within 90 days of death
Q.e: The designation is made by ticking the box on the estate’s first T3. The executor can choose a year-end within 12 months of death, which allows income to be timed and split between tax years.

Q.q: When is the T3 due, and what is the penalty for a late one?
o: 90 days after year-end; $25 per day, minimum $100, maximum $2,500
60 days after year-end; $50 per day, minimum $250, maximum $5,000
90 days after death; 5 percent of the balance plus 1 percent per month
180 days after year-end; $25 per day with no minimum or maximum
Q.e: The T3 and any tax owing are due 90 days after the estate’s year-end, or after final distribution if the trust ends. A late T3 draws $25 per day, minimum $100, maximum $2,500, even if no tax is owing.

Q.q: How many graduated rate estates are allowed for one person, and what record advice does the chapter give?
o: One for each will signed; keep records only until the T3 return is filed
Two, one for each spouse named; keep records for one year after the death
One for each province involved; keep records only if the CRA asks for them
One, even with several wills; keep returns, valuations, assessments, and receipts for years
Q.e: Only one graduated rate estate is allowed per person, even with several wills. Keep the final return, T3s, valuations, assessments, and receipts until the estate closes and for some time afterward, as the best defence in a review.

Q.q: Why is a clearance certificate the most important protection, and what is the executor’s exposure without it?
o: It cancels all tax owing by the estate; personal liability up to the executor’s fee
It confirms the will is valid; personal liability up to the probate fee
It shifts remaining liability to the estate and recipients; personal liability up to the value distributed
It confirms the beneficiaries’ share; personal liability up to the funeral costs
Q.e: If an executor distributes while the CRA is owed money, the executor is personally liable up to the value distributed. A clearance certificate confirms the tax is paid or secured and shifts remaining liability to the estate and recipients.

Q.q: When should the executor apply for the certificate, and which form is used?
o: After all returns are filed and taxes paid or secured; the TX19, sent separately
With the returns, to speed up the assessment; the T3 form, sent together
Before the final return, to fix the amount owing; the TX19, sent with the T3
After distribution, to correct any errors found; the T1 form, sent separately
Q.e: The executor applies only after all required returns are filed and assessed, any reassessments are resolved, and all taxes are paid or secured. The request is made on the TX19 and should not be submitted with the returns, because that delays assessment.

Q.q: Roughly how long does the CRA take, and what do patient executors do?
o: Acknowledgement within 120 days and assessment up to 45 days; full distribution at once
Acknowledgement within 28 days and assessment up to 90 days; no distribution until two years pass
Acknowledgement within 12 days and assessment up to 36 months; partial distributions without a reserve
Acknowledgement within 45 days and assessment up to 120 days; partial distributions with a reserve
Q.e: The CRA sends an acknowledgement within 45 days, and the assessment can take up to 120 days or longer if an audit is needed. Executors who plan for this wait can make partial distributions, holding back a reserve for taxes and expenses.

Q.q: In Quebec, what must the liquidator obtain before distributing, and what may be paid first?
o: A certificate of clearance from the CRA only; any expense without limit
A court order from the Superior Court; funeral costs of $5,000 only
A notice from the land register; heating and insurance bills after distribution
A certificate authorizing distribution from Revenu Québec; urgent expenses up to $12,000
Q.e: The liquidator must obtain a certificate authorizing distribution from Revenu Québec before distributing property or income, whatever its value. Before the certificate is issued, urgent expenses of up to $12,000 for the death or the property may be paid, and a partial certificate may be issued.

Q.e: Once the certificates are received, the executor can distribute the residue, prepare a final account, ask the beneficiaries to sign releases, and close the estate account. Part II then provides practice tests, with answers and short explanations, to check what you have learned.
